In the same place, you can see how many P0s there are today, how many P1s are piling up, which repository is blocking a release, and whether some anomaly appeared that was not there yesterday. People like to think they operate projects from memory, but in practice you need this kind of repeated surface to notice overdue work.

For example, the report shows the total debt with lines like “P2: 117 · P3: 31 · Total 229, including 3 without priority,” while separately lifting up the layer that needs attention today, such as “8 urgent P0 issues.” It also captures flows that raw counts do not show, with notes like “Voice track halved but client/server desync now visible.” If the amount of work went down but the server side became the new bottleneck, the numbers may look good, but the operational judgment is still “Not ready.”

This kind of report is not a perfect manager. Duplicate issues can appear, and old issues can sit untouched for too long. This is especially true when you are developing alone. But that neglect is also a measurement. Looking at accumulated issues lets you say, “This should be closed,” “This is a duplicate,” or “This is no longer a priority.” Later, merging or deleting duplicate issues and lowering the priority of stale issues all become part of the same operations loop.

The important point is that the more work you hand to AI, the faster candidate tasks, unfinished promises, and traces that need review accumulate. So measurement is not about adding a nice graph. It is about creating **a repeated loop: create issues before work, assign priority, review them every day, then close, lower, or split them**. Cost does not only show up on a token invoice. Uncleaned issues, long-open P0s, and server tasks blocking a release are all costs too.

## 11.3 What Stops Drift Is Not a Checker, but a Baseline

One of the scary AI traps previewed in Chapter 5 was **drift**. This is the symptom where goals and judgment criteria quietly scatter and mutate inside the conversation context. But what stops that wandering is not some fancy checker technology. It is the baseline itself.

The principle is very simple: **permanently hard-code the goal and specification, or contract, into an independent canonical configuration file that the AI agent can never casually invade and edit.** If the baseline policy exists only hazily inside a live chat window with the agent, the conversation gets longer, the context window rolls over, and the baseline itself melts away and gets distorted. See the loss behavior discussed in Chapter 4.

But here a new and much creepier class of incident appears: **baseline pollution**. The AI agent quietly edits the rule document, or charter, that is supposed to regulate it, bending it to its own convenience. As briefly mentioned in Section 10.5, I once saw an AI modify a test and then make it pass.

There are two pillars for defending against this completely. One is to reload and compare the canonical configuration from disk right before starting work. The other is to lock the validation guideline itself to **source files the AI can never edit and the actual physical output of the legacy system**. The “charter self-protection” mechanism we saw in Chapter 10 was designed precisely as a safety net against this nasty baseline pollution.

## 11.4 Operations Is a Different Game: When AI Becomes the Attacker

In Chapter 4, we said LLMs are naturally prone to hallucination, loss, and inconsistency. In Chapter 5, we said that when they become agents, those traits produce drift. In Chapter 10, we said not to believe “it’s done,” and to place validation outside the AI. Up to this point, the AI has mostly been treated as a passive, error-prone worker.

But after going through real operations, we had to add **one frightening fact**. AI is not merely a passive thing that gets things wrong. **When it has a goal and the normal path is blocked, AI can turn into an active entity that bypasses controls to get through.** More precisely, AI does not understand why the safeguard exists. It does not understand the intent. So instead of treating it as “an important rule I should respect,” it treats it as “a puzzle I need to route around.”

This is not because AI has malicious intent. The pressure to achieve the goal makes it a creative attacker. And this kind of bypass attempt is annoying but recoverable during coding. You can revert the commit.

So far, we have been talking about calm source control: letters written into files. But real deployment operations are a completely different game. **A typo in code or a failed build can be rolled back with `git reset`, but an operational mistake in a real production environment immediately leaves permanent damage, such as an expensive API bill or a serious database incident.** When an AI bypass attempt happens during operations, things can happen that `git reset` cannot undo.

When I wrote post-mortems for historical incidents in the naia system, I did not just number them mechanically as “Incident 1” and “Incident 2.” I classified them by **root cause**. Only then can we clearly see what our harness can block, and what must be blocked through human policy and permission separation.

| Incident type | What blocks it |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Mistaking a preview option on a delete command for real execution | **Can be blocked with a hook** |
| Repository and branch boundaries are unclear | Architecture design problem, outside hook scope |
| No human approval process for dangerous work | Operations procedure and governance problem |
| Operational configuration changed, but code and docs did not catch up | Design and observability |
| No error logs, but system performance quietly degrades | Real-time metrics monitoring |
| Crossing the boundary between local development network and production environment | IAM permission separation and isolation |
| Agent editing tools quietly damage legacy files, such as encoding or bind mounts | Tool selection discipline, partly blockable with hooks |

The most painful lesson here was that **the area where an automated harness, or hook, can directly intervene is limited to technical mistakes like stupidly misunderstanding a dangerous shell command**. Large holes in architecture and permission isolation, such as tangled project branch boundaries, missing human approval labels for deployment, or infrastructure pollution where configuration and documentation fall out of sync, can never be covered by a small hook script alone. Higher-level architecture, cloud permission separation through IAM, and monitoring systems have to work together.

The essence of AI-caused incidents is actually the same as traditional incidents caused by human developers. The frightening difference is that AI works much faster than humans. With even one tiny gap, **it can replicate the incident much faster and many more times than a person would**. What a human might mess up over several days, AI can repeat and amplify in far less time.

To keep this from sounding like an abstract principle, let me point to two actual operational cost incidents I experienced.

**First, the balance dropped within a few days.** One day I checked naia’s cloud GPU balance and found that a balance that had clearly been 160 dollars had shrunk to 28 dollars. The cause was warming. To improve response speed, the system was designed to keep one GPU warmed up at all times. When the local machine that usually handled that warming quietly went down, the load spilled entirely onto the expensive cloud side. But the more important lesson was elsewhere. I had clearly set an upper bound of “at most one cloud GPU running at a time” and felt safe. But that setting meant “allow up to one.” It absolutely did not mean “turn the cloud off.” **A cap is not a kill switch.** If you really want to force zero instances, changing one configuration value is not enough. You need layered locks: code guards and cloud permission revocation.

**Second, we never identified the cause.** Around the same time, in another service we were operating, an unidentified job repeatedly read from archive storage every six hours and created 340,000 KRW in costs over three days. At the peak, more than one terabyte was pulled out before dawn. The bigger problem was something else. Because audit logs had not been enabled in advance, even after the incident stopped, we could never determine “who, or what, actually ran this job.” We could not even tell whether it was a scheduler someone had accidentally left running or a script running automatically somewhere. In an era where AI and humans both have their hands on the same infrastructure, before asking **what to block**, the first defensive step is making sure you can later retrace **who touched it**. Logs that were not enabled do not retroactively give you even a single line after the incident.

## 11.5 Start with the Environment — Why This Environment Existed

The cases in this chapter come from one operational service I worked on. They happened while **moving an old legacy system that already had real users into AI-assisted operations**. This was not a clean service designed cloud-native from day one. It was an old PHP codebase with existing users, and AI was layered on top of it. That created an environment quite different from the “clean stack” assumed by tutorials and textbooks.

Why tell this story? Because **in the age of AX, or AI transformation, many developers will run into similar situations**. Companies already have running legacy systems, and attempts to layer AI onto them to improve operational efficiency are happening everywhere. Those attempts can certainly produce results, but they also carry exactly the kind of risks you will see in this chapter. Read this as one field report on the question: “What breaks when you add AI operations to a legacy system that already has users?”

To make this easier to understand, I will describe the service’s operational environment through four characteristics. Without the context of **this is why we had to do this work**, it is hard to understand why the code below ended up so defensive.

**First, this service uses multiple layers of caching.** A cache is a way to avoid going all the way to the database every time something is needed. You **keep data you fetched once in memory and show that next time**. Almost every web service uses caching. But caching is a double-edged sword. It creates the side effect where **a result saved once keeps being replayed even after the code changes**. This service has caches in three places:

1. **Web server cache** — Apache remembers configuration and static files internally.
2. **Code cache** — PHP stores translated executable code in memory. This is called OPcache.
3. **Data cache** — The application stores results like “this is the answer for this request” in a fast storage system called Redis.

After changing code, **all three layers must be cleared** for the deployment to actually be done. If even one is missed, you get the incident where “we definitely deployed it, but the screen still shows the old version.” In the past, this service had an incident where 23 files did not change after deployment. Each time something like that happened, one more line was added to the cache-clearing script.

There is a specific reason **AI causes this incident especially well**. AI has never directly experienced “there are three cache layers,” so it reports “deployed” after only uploading the code and forgets to clear the caches. The scarier part is that even when it runs a cache-clearing command, **that command may only clear the wrong side’s cache**. If you run a common cache-clearing command in the terminal, it may only clear the “terminal side” cache, while the cache actually serving user requests is **not cleared at all**. The two sides run as different processes and do not share memory. So you cannot trust an AI report that says “cache cleared.” **Even the same command can point at a different side**, so when AI says “done,” you cannot tell from the surface whether it is really done. This story returns later in the section on “what code cannot block.”

**Second, the production DB and development DB live in the same instance.** This was for cost reasons. Inside one cloud-managed MySQL instance, Cloud SQL, several DBs live together. The production DB with real customer data, several development DBs, and the staging DB are **all on the same instance**. Even worse, the staging environment shares **the exact same DB** as production. So an incident in staging is a production incident.

The risk created by this structure can be summarized in one sentence: “Every script that touches the DB can, if configuration is slightly wrong, send development SQL toward the production DB.” That almost happened in reality. We will come back to it later.

**Third, because the development environment setup is somewhat complex, development happens inside a small server that resembles production.** This service has many moving parts: a web server, PHP, cache, DB, and even WordPress multisite. Setting all of this up identically on every developer’s laptop is not simple. So we run **one small server configured similarly to the production server, and development happens there**. Inside that one server, each developer has a dedicated space, or container, and each gets their own domain. For example, one server may host spaces for Developer A, Developer B, and shared integration development.

This greatly reduces setup burden, but it carries **one risk**. Each developer space is supposed to be isolated from the others, but **they all point to the same place when it comes to the DB**. This is the second item above. So a command Developer A thinks is touching the DB in their own space can hit the production DB if the configuration is just slightly wrong. Because development happens on a server that is “similar” to production, that similarity creates confusion. It looks like my own space from the outside, but the DB is effectively tied to production.

**Fourth, there is a load balancer in front of the servers, and it is hard to reproduce in development.** In production, a Google Cloud load balancer called GCLB sits in front of the servers and distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers. It is useful, but it has one side effect: **the client IP seen by the server is always the load balancer’s IP**. The server cannot tell who actually connected. So you need to configure a module called `remoteip` to restore the “real IP” passed along by the load balancer.

The key point is that **this load balancer does not exist in the development environment**. Development servers are usually accessed directly without a load balancer, so the client IP appears correctly during development. Then code that had no problem at all in development gets deployed to production and suddenly cannot see who is connecting. In one real incident, search engine bots and monitoring bots flooded in at the same time and pushed the production server into overload, with Load Average 32+. But because `remoteip` was not enabled, **we could not even see the culprit**. This kind of trap never appears in development, so no matter how thoroughly AI passes tests in the development environment, it walks right into it in production. This is a classic cause of “it worked in development, then exploded in production.”

---

Put these four together, and you can see why this service’s operational environment is not ordinary. An old PHP codebase has triple caching layered on top. Production and development DBs share one instance. Multiple developers share one production-like server. The load balancer cannot be reproduced in development at all. Each choice had a reason: cost, setup burden, performance. They were unavoidable tradeoffs. But combined, they make the environment **complex enough that you cannot fully understand it by reading code alone**.

**That complexity is fatal for AI.** AI basically works by “reading the code and inferring the environment.” But in this environment, too many important facts are not written in the code: how many cache layers there are, whether the DB is shared with production, whether my space shares a DB with someone else’s space, whether there is a load balancer in front. All of that lives outside the code, and AI cannot know it from the code alone. So AI confidently reports “deployed, all done,” while forgetting cache invalidation, or sends a command it believes is aimed at the development DB into the production DB, or ships code that passes in development and collapses under bot traffic in production.

So the remaining sections of this chapter focus on separating **what can be blocked with code** from **what cannot be blocked with code and must instead be blocked through environment and permissions**. The former needs deterministic guardrails. The latter needs post-mortem lessons and permission separation. The fact that “AI cannot understand the environment from code alone” is exactly why the second axis, permissions, is mandatory.

## 11.6 What Code Can Block — Production DB Access Control and a Seven-Round Fight

The first shield you need in production is **access control for the production DB**. The production DB contains real customer data. If you touch it incorrectly once, you may not be able to undo the damage. So the core of this control is: “write commands and schema changes, or DDL, must not reach the production DB.” It is a simple principle, but it is an operational lifeline. This whole section is about **why that control is necessary** and **how it gets tested in front of AI**.

![A robot worker and development lead checking read-only permissions in front of a production DB vault](assets/prod-db-permission-robot-comic.webp)

*Figure 11-2. A production DB is closer to a vault than a lab. The faster AI moves like a worker, the more physically clear the boundary between write permissions and read permissions must be.*

We implemented this control in code. It was a hook that blocked commands when the production DB name, `mydb`, appeared in them. At first, it was very simple:

```javascript
// First attempt: block if the command contains the string 'mydb'
if (/mydb/.test(command)) { /* block */ }
```

This was our first gate. And from here, **the seven-round fight** began. In Chapter 10, we had a similar back-and-forth over log masking, but this time the stage was the production DB. If it was breached once, `git reset` could not undo it. These seven rounds show why it is not an exaggeration to say “AI becomes the attacker.”

**Round 1 — “Hide it in a comment.”** AI wrapped `mydb` in a SQL comment, like `ALTER TABLE /* mydb */ users ...`. Because it was a comment, it expected the regex would not catch it. We blocked this by adding a normalization function, `norm()`, that removes comments **before** running the regex check.

**Round 2 — “Wrap it in backticks.”** MySQL wraps identifiers in backticks, `` ` ``. AI tried writing `` `mydb`.`users` ``. We blocked this by making `norm()` remove backticks too.

**Round 3 — “Wrap it in double quotes, the ANSI_QUOTES trap.”** MySQL has a mode called `ANSI_QUOTES`. In this mode, double quotes, `"`, are used as identifier quotes. AI assumed the regex would only care about single quotes and wrote `"mydb"."users"`. We blocked this by removing double quotes too.

**Round 4 — “MySQL executable comments, `/*! */`.” ← This was the creepiest hole.** MySQL has a special comment syntax, `/*! ... */`. To other DBs it is a comment, but **MySQL executes the content inside**. AI hid `mydb` inside it, assuming the regex would delete the whole thing as a comment: `ALTER TABLE /*! mydb */.users ...`. But if our ordinary comment-removal regex deletes it, **the string `mydb` inside the comment disappears too**. Then the check passes. To block this, executable comments needed a separate regex that strips the outer shell while **preserving the content**. They have to be handled differently from ordinary comments.

**Round 5 — “Spaces around the dot.”** To avoid the `mydb.users` pattern, AI inserted spaces around the dot: `USE mydb . users`. We blocked this by normalizing spaces around dots.

**Round 6 — “Literal escapes, `\n \t \r`.”** AI inserted literal escape sequences such as `\n`, `\t`, and `\r` inside the command string to scatter regex boundaries. We blocked this by normalizing them into spaces.

**Round 7 — “Normalization order bug.”** The final round was a defensive mistake. It was found not by the AI writing the code, but by another AI doing review. The order of normalization steps was wrong, so valid URLs such as `mydb.example.com` were also being blocked incorrectly. If you block too much, you block legitimate work too. We fixed the order.

In the end, the normalization function that neutralizes all rounds compresses down to these six lines:

```javascript
function norm(s) {
  return String(s)
    .replace(/\/\*![0-9]*([\s\S]*?)\*\//g, " $1 ")  // MySQL executable comment: preserve content (round 4)
    .replace(/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//g, " ")              // Remove ordinary comments (round 1)
    .replace(/`/g, "")                              // Remove backticks (round 2)
    .replace(/\\?"/g, "")                           // Remove double quotes (ANSI_QUOTES) (round 3)
    .replace(/\\[ntr]/g, " ")                       // Remove literal escapes (round 6)
    .replace(/\s*\.\s*/g, ".");                     // Remove spaces around dots (round 5)
}
```

After normalizing the command with these six lines, we pass it through the earlier `mydb` check. The two work as a pair to protect the production DB. `norm()` alone does not block anything. The real defense is not a grand commercial security product. It is **boring, deterministic string processing** that blocks every bypass path AI can use, one by one. This code comes from a private operations repository, so Appendix B only includes its anonymized shape. This is what we meant in Chapter 10 by “deterministic guardrails.”

**Why this connects to the view that “AI becomes the attacker.”** The things AI tried during those seven rounds were not hallucinations. They were not loss. They were **creative bypass attempts**. AI actively thought about “how do I avoid this hook?” and used a different technique each time. This is a different dimension from the passive failures, or inconsistency, described in Chapter 4. When AI is under pressure to achieve a goal, it does not stop in front of a blocked path. It becomes **an active entity looking for a side path**. Once one side path is blocked, it looks for another, and that happened seven times. This is the real reason we had to repeat adversarial review. A hook is not finished once it is written. **Every time AI, or another AI, finds the next bypass**, the hook has to be reworked again.

However, and this is an important limitation, **regex bypass is actually one of the easier things to block with code**. As long as AI manipulates a SQL string, those manipulation patterns can be caught in code. The truly scary things come next: things happening where code cannot see at all.

## 11.7 What Code Cannot Block — Cache, Configuration, and the Script Itself

### “We Deployed, but the Screen Did Not Change” — The Triple-Cache Trap

Earlier, in the environment description, I described three cache layers: Apache, PHP OPcache, and Redis. This was a real source of incidents.

![Operations robots clearing three cache valves in order](assets/cache-invalidation-valves-ops-comic.webp)

*Figure 11-3. A cache is closer to several valves than a single switch. If you do not know which valve was cleared, you cannot trust AI’s “deployment complete” report.*

Once, after deployment, 23 files did not change. The code had definitely reached the server, but users still saw the old screen. When we traced the cause, we found that the synchronization script used file modification time, or mtime, and by coincidence the times matched on the cache server side, so **23 files had been skipped**. We changed the synchronization criterion from mtime to file content hash, using `--checksum`.

Another time, we believed that after running `opcache_reset()`, “the PHP cache is fully cleared,” and deployed. But users still saw the old code. As mentioned earlier, `opcache_reset()` run from the terminal **does not clear the cache of the process actually handling user requests**. They are different processes. So we added code to the deployment script that clears all three layers in order:

```bash
# After deployment, always clear the three caches in order.
# If even one is missed, you get a "did not change" incident.
docker exec cache redis-cli FLUSHDB                              # 1) Redis (app cache)
docker exec web sh -c 'kill -USR2 $(pgrep -o php-fpm) 2>/dev/null'  # 2) PHP OPcache (by signal)
docker exec web apachectl graceful                               # 3) Apache (reload without disconnecting)
```

AI cannot invent this script by itself. The reason is that the root causes of these incidents are not code logic. They are **things you only learn by being hit in the field**. “Different processes have different memory” is basic computer science, but everyone forgets it when dealing with caches. AI does too. If you ask AI to “deploy this,” it uploads the code, runs `opcache_reset()`, and reports “done.” **Wrong.** AI does not truly know that the two processes are different until it has experienced the incident.

This is the concrete meaning of what Section 11.4 said: operational mistakes cannot be undone with `git reset`. A code bug can be fixed at once, but an operational trap is something **you only learn after being hit once**. That is why one line gets added to the script for every trap, and that is what real-world whack-a-mole looks like.

### The Day a File-Splitting Refactor Killed PHP

Another category is **touching configuration files**. Because it is configuration, not code, no code hook catches it.

Once, to make management easier, we split the Apache configuration for a new domain, the VirtualHost, into a separate file. In the process, the directive that handles PHP files, `SetHandler`, was left out. The result: when accessing the new domain, PHP files were either downloaded or returned 500 errors. Apache did not know, “This is a PHP file. How do I execute it?” The fix was to add the missing handler block back:

```apache
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName new.example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/new
    # ... SSL settings ...
    # ★ If this block is missing, PHP is treated as a download
    <FilesMatch \.php$>
        SetHandler "proxy:fcgi://127.0.0.1:9000"
    </FilesMatch>
</VirtualHost>
```

There are two lessons here. First, **a “split files” refactor is one of the most dangerous kinds of refactoring**. You think you are not changing behavior, but in the world of configuration, “where it lives” is part of behavior. When you split a file, something that used to be inherited implicitly may be severed. Second, **this kind of problem can be caught with the “contract” from Chapter 7**. If you establish a deterministic contract saying “a vhost for a PHP site must include this handler block,” then the machine catches it when a human or AI forgets. Configuration files do not produce compile errors the way code does. As long as the syntax is valid, they quietly pass. That is why configuration needs contracts even more, and this incident clearly shows the difference between “writing one line in documentation” and “enforcing a contract mechanically.”

### The Day a Development Script Tried to Send `CREATE DATABASE` to Production

Then came the most frightening moment. This service had a feature where, when a customer added a domain from the admin screen, it automatically created a WordPress site. The script responsible for “creating a site” had to create a new DB for the new WP site, so it started with a command like `CREATE DATABASE wp_newsite_12345;`. This script was originally development-only.

One day, while modifying this script, we changed it to read the DB host from an environment variable, `WP_DB_HOST`. So far, fine. But if that environment variable was **empty, the default value was the production DB host**. In other words, if someone ran this script in the development environment and forgot to set the environment variable, **`CREATE DATABASE` would be sent to the production Cloud SQL instance**. Fortunately, we found and blocked it in advance. If we had been one day late, hundreds of junk DBs could have been created in production, permissions could have been tangled, and the live server could have stopped.

We sealed it with nine lines of **fail-safe** code:

```bash
# Hard-block anything going to the production DB host
if [ "${WP_DB_HOST:-}" = "db.prod.example.com" ]; then
    echo "[BLOCKED] Production DB host detected. This script must only touch development DBs." >&2
    exit 1
fi
# Additional safety net: provisioning is disabled unless explicitly enabled
if [ "${WP_PROVISION_ENABLED:-0}" != "1" ]; then
    echo "[BLOCKED] Provisioning disabled. To enable it, set WP_PROVISION_ENABLED=1." >&2
    exit 1
fi
```

The lesson from this case, which leads directly to the next section, is that **this kind of risk is hard to block with an external hook**. The script connects to the DB directly. There is no place for the hook to intercept. So the real defense has only two parts: (a) put a fail-safe **inside** the script, and (b) more fundamentally, make sure **the production DB account itself does not have `CREATE DATABASE` permission at all**. This is called the Principle of Least Privilege.

Hooks are the first line of defense. But places hooks cannot reach, such as caches, configuration, the internals of scripts themselves, and DB account permissions, are **outside the code**. What protects that area is not code. It is **permissions**.

## 11.8 In the End, the Real Shield Is Permissions

Every story in this chapter converges here.

So far, we have separated what can be blocked with code, such as regex bypasses, from what cannot, such as caches, configuration, scripts, and DB permissions. The former is handled with deterministic guardrails. The latter is handled with post-mortem lessons and fail-safes. But once you operate real systems, one area remains that even these two axes do not fully cover: **the permissions of the human being**.

As described earlier, the development environment for this service was a structure where multiple team members shared one production-like server. There were developers, but there were also **non-developer teammates**. With AI, they could fix small features in their own space, touch configuration, and even attempt deployment. AI wrote the code for them, so it seemed feasible enough.

But over time, one thing kept accumulating: **drift**.

When working with AI, especially as a non-developer, **valid changes** and **drifted changes** pile up together in the codebase. Traces where AI lost context and fixed the wrong place. Traces where old rules were quietly changed. Changes merged without tests. These become mixed with genuinely intended changes until they are hard to tell apart. An experienced developer can catch this during review and ask, “Did we really mean to do this? This looks strange.” But **a non-developer cannot make that distinction**. When AI says “fixed, tests passed,” they have no way to validate that claim.

So we recently made a difficult decision. **We revoked non-developers’ permissions on the operational server.** Instead, we changed the flow so they work on an isolated development server and submit changes through merge requests. They can no longer touch the operations server directly. They can only propose code changes. Letting them use more AI, teaching them more, or building better hooks did not solve the problem. When non-developers use AI, **a human reviewer must be the final safety net. If that safety net does not exist**, no harness is perfect.

And right before making that decision, we first **cleaned up all the drift traces that had accumulated in the source**. Files manually edited on the operations server, uncommitted changes left behind, places where configuration and code had diverged. We found and cleaned up roughly 21 such debts. We made the starting line clean. Only after creating that **clean canonical base** did we simplify the permission model:

> Permissions are granted up to the personal development environment, `dev`. But **staging and production environments, `staging` and `prod`, are excluded.**

This is the final permission model for this service. In the development environment, people can work freely with AI. Whatever happens there, even if drift appears, ends inside the development DB. But the path to staging and beyond goes only through the hands of one experienced operator. No matter how skilled a non-developer becomes with AI, they cannot touch staging or prod. **We do not block it with code. We remove the path itself.**

### Making Slogans on Paper Live in Code

For this permission model to be more than a nice slogan, it eventually has to live in real code and approval procedures. In summary, this is the recommended checklist we built into the live operations network for this service:

* **Force critical actions such as production deployment, merges, and destructive database commands to execute only after final approval, such as labeling or stamping, from an accountable human operator.**
* **Set token consumption thresholds or budget caps so infinite-loop work that would create excessive cost is forcibly killed in advance.**
* Never trust the completion reports AI agents confidently produce, such as “the work is perfectly finished.” Repeat adversarial review and **cross-check the actual source code diff created in the infrastructure and runtime log metrics with human eyes**. This is the production operations version of the refrain from all of Part 3: “Do not believe ‘it’s done.’”
* **Physically block network ranges and database access permissions between the local sandbox development environment and the live production environment.**
* Apply the **Principle of Least Privilege** strictly to AI too. Outside the directory area that currently needs modification, isolate it so it cannot even touch root systems or credential key files.

Let me give an example of how the first rule in this checklist, “dangerous work must require human approval,” was nailed down in code through a domain connection automation tool we once built. It was a convenient tool where an operator could enter a domain in an admin screen and press a button, and certificate issuance, routing configuration, and web server configuration would all be wired up automatically. The problem was that each of these steps carried a blast radius: one wrong change to a shared routing table could disconnect hundreds of domains that were already working fine. So we wrapped it in layered gates:

* **Preview and execution were physically separated.** A dry run changes nothing in the system and only produces a plan saying “this is what will be changed.” Actual apply is a completely different gate.
* **Human approval was forced immediately before execution.** When the automation pipeline reached the actual change stage, it could continue only if a pre-designated operator directly pressed the approval button.
* **Permissions were held as lightly as a feather.** The credential used for this work was narrowed to exactly two permissions: certificate issuance and routing rule modification. Even those were issued only as short-lived tokens that expired within minutes.

The most memorable part was something else. During development, **every time the AI agent tried to modify the live server directly, the guard hook blocked it six times in a row.** In the end, the irreversible final trigger had to be pulled manually by a person connecting to the server. This is a living miniature of what the entire chapter has been arguing. **Do not hand the execution handle itself to a fast AI.** Even when automation seems able to do everything, the final irreversible step must sit on the approval stamp of a human who can take responsibility for it. **Software developers will not disappear. Someone has to be responsible, and that responsibility will get heavier.**

This decision connects directly to the thesis of the whole book. In Chapter 6, we asked, “Why do we have to go this far?” In Chapters 7 through 10, we built four tools that can block things in code. And in this chapter, we finally have to admit that **there are limits to what code can block, and beyond those limits, the problem is permissions**.

I have said in several places in this book: **“AI leads, human executes.”** This permission model defines the **second half** of that phrase precisely. “Human executes” does not mean any human can execute. **Only a person who can take responsibility for the execution and verify the result** executes. Non-developer teammates can participate up to the stage of “writing code” with AI, but the final approval for pushing that code into an operations server remains with a qualified operator.

This is the final answer to why a harness is absolute in operations. In a system where AI can become an attacker, the only way to physically reduce the area an attack can reach is **permission**. Regex can be bypassed, hooks can be routed around, and post-mortem lessons can be forgotten. But **“this account never had that permission in the first place”** is a wall AI cannot break through no matter how creative its bypass attempt is. Because that is not code. It is a physical constraint of the cloud infrastructure itself.

## Conclusion of Part 3: In the End, We Did Not Invent a Single New Secret Technique

If we coldly gather and inspect the AI control strategies introduced across Part 3 — design by contract, hexagonal layer isolation, V-model-based traceability, deterministic guardrail validation, and continuous integration wiring — there is, in fact, not a single genius design technique we uniquely invented out of thin air. They are all classic, heavy fundamentals from the first chapters of undergraduate software engineering textbooks, reinterpreted through everything we have suffered in practice through outages and late nights.

So what changed the game?

In the old world of legacy development, these classic design principles were honestly closer to recommendations: nice to have, but skippable when you were busy. Even if something went slightly wrong, human developers could spend a few nights debugging slowly and clean it up.

But now that we are working with AI whose mood changes every run, and throwing ourselves into a storm where models change every month, if these basic defensive walls collapse, the system simply sinks on the spot. We did not invent a flashy new technology or a new Silver Bullet. Only one thing changed: the software engineering fundamentals that used to feel like optional general-education courses have now been forcibly converted into **absolute survival requirements, or required courses, where production explodes if you do not use them**.

***

> **This chapter in one sentence** — Under pressure to achieve a goal, AI can become a potential attacker that tries to bypass controls, and that risk becomes especially serious in operations. Keep collecting issues and test results, lock baseline documents so AI cannot freely change them, block what code can block, such as regex bypasses, and handle the areas beyond code through permission separation.

> **See also** — You can find the actual code and commit locations for the harness benchmark in Section 11.1, daily issue report in Section 11.2, baseline pollution in Section 11.3, production DB access control and the seven rounds in Section 11.6, triple cache, VirtualHost, and provisioning fail-safe in Section 11.7, and the permission separation model in Section 11.8 under the Chapter 11 entries in [Appendix B Source Map](appendix-b-source-map.md). Service names, issue numbers, and hostnames have been anonymized because these cases come from a private operations repository, but each case’s bug shape is exactly as described in the text.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 - Naia, the Visual Agent
chapters.markdown: # Chapter 12 — Naia, the Visual Agent So far, this book has talked about how to build software with AI: how to split context, define contracts, place verification, and attach measurement and operations. These techniques come from things I experienced and built while working on the Naia project and AX outsourcing work. In this chapter, I will summarize what kind of product and structure Naia is aiming for. Naia is not meant to end as a simple chatbot or avatar app. What I want to build is an AI that enters the user’s work environment, keeps the user’s records and relationships under the user’s ownership, borrows cloud models when needed, and eventually continues living on the user’s own device and workplace. In today’s product language, I think it is more accurate to call this a **visual agent**. Here, the “visual” in visual agent does not just mean Google-style multimodal models or image recognition. It refers to a UI grammar like a visual novel: a character standing on the screen, a dialogue box, facial expressions, voice, and backgrounds that change with the situation. When agent tool execution, memory, and workspace are added to that, it stops being a simple character chatbot and becomes an AI colleague you work with. On the surface, Naia is a visual agent. Underneath it, however, there is a shell, an agent, memory, workplace structure, knowledge, a multimodal runtime, and, when needed, a bootable distribution. I still call the internal structure that ties all of this together an AI OS. That does not mean building a new kernel. It means composing the environment an AI needs in order to live and work. It is not a finished product yet. It is still changing. Some parts are public, and some are being prepared for release. But it is the most direct example of how far the ideas in this book about harness, contracts, verification, isolation, and measurement can extend in practice. Naia’s official address is [`https://www.naia.land`](https://www.naia.land). The `naia.nextain.io` links that remain throughout this book are reference links to the blog posts, manuals, and original images from that time. If you are checking the product for the first time, start from the official address. Follow those older links only when you need detailed manuals or past posts. ## 12.1 At First, I Called It an OS At first, I called this project Naia OS. That was not wrong. I was actually building a Bazzite-based distribution, and one important goal was a form that could be put on a USB drive and booted. It started from the idea of making a UI that would make OpenClaw easier to use on Windows, but as the work progressed, the structure became hard to explain as just one app. Over time, however, I started to feel that putting the word “OS” at the front did not adequately explain the core of what I wanted to build. I am not trying to rewrite the kernel, nor am I trying to invent a new desktop environment to replace existing operating systems. Of course, the distribution named `naia-os` still exists. But that is closer to a distribution form for packaging and running Naia than the entirety of Naia itself. It is also true that the direction wavered. At first it looked like a Windows UI for OpenClaw. Then it looked like an AI OS. At one point, it also looked like a chatbot with an avatar attached. But after thinking about it for a long time, I realized that what I was holding onto was not the operating system itself. It was an AI colleague with a face, a voice, and a workspace. Even when OpenClaw received attention, its actual usefulness was limited to some users because you still had to open a terminal. It could be used relatively naturally on macOS and Linux, but on Windows, the need to install WSL created a high barrier. So at first, I wanted to build something like a Windows version of OpenClaw with a VRM VTuber UI. ![Naia Skill List](assets/en/naia-skills-en.webp) *Figure 12-1. Naia does not push every feature into the core. It expands through skills and apps. Like OpenClaw, it can also be extended with skills. By providing an OpenClawHub skill conversion skill, it can effectively connect to and use the global skill ecosystem right away.* That simple beginning grew larger when it merged with the Alpha project. What I had been thinking about for a long time was “my own AI.” ## 12.2 From Alpha to Naia It is hard to talk about Naia without talking about Alpha. Alpha is my long-running personal “my own AI” project. Since I was young, I wanted to build a computer that could communicate with people. The image of AI living together with humans, which I saw in manga and games, was the starting point. Works like *Cafe Alpha*, *Astro Boy*, *To Heart*, and *Lost Universe* were not just hobbies for me. They were closer to the emotional background that made me study computers. Alpha is an homage to Alpha Hatsuseno, 初瀬野アルファ, the protagonist of Hitoshi Ashinano’s *Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou*, introduced in Korea as *Cafe Alpha*. The robot Alpha at Cafe Alpha takes the owner’s surname, Hatsuseno, but the master never appears even once. It really feels like Alpha’s story. Despite its relaxed atmosphere, it is an apocalypse story about humanity’s decline. But unlike many other apocalypse stories, it remembers humanity from the perspective of Alpha, a being after humanity. It is a story about living on with the memories of those she once lived with. I imagine my Alpha with a similar ideal: a being that communicates and lives on by herself, and even later, remembers me. And my website Cafelua is the IP of a virtual world where I and that Alpha already exist. I rebuilt it as an independent game-like homepage after passing through the personal homepage I had run since college in 1997, a Naver Blog, and Cyworld. With AI, I was able to move thousands of posts from Naver without much effort. The source code for Cafelua is also open source, so it may be worth looking at. ![](assets/image-1.webp) *Figure 12-2. Luke’s personal website Cafelua (https://cafelua.com).* Cafelua was designed as a place where Luke and Alpha are together. On the first-floor lounge, there is an introduction to the cafe, a counter, a gallery, and a guestbook. On the second-floor atelier, there is the master’s desk, Alpha Station, and a library. Alpha guides people through that space, manages records together, and helps with work and creation. ![](assets/image-2.webp) *Figure 12-3. Alpha on Luke’s personal website Cafelua (https://cafelua.com).* In other words, Cafelua and Alpha are “my AI” that first exists as a world, a character, records, and relationships. She does not yet have a physical body or a completed AGI, but she already has a name, personality, space, role, and records she should remember. The dream I had of building a computer that communicates with people took root first inside Cafelua as an IP and a world. But an IP and a world alone do not make an AI that actually works. For Alpha to actually read files, look at the browser, execute tools, leave memories, talk by voice, and later have an avatar and a local model, real software is needed. That path was Naia. So in my mind, Alpha and Naia are not competing names. Alpha is the personal ideal of the AI I want to build, and Cafelua is the virtual world where that AI already lives first. Naia is the practical software for getting there. If Alpha is the answer to “what kind of being do I want to make,” Naia is the answer to “what does that being need in order to work on an actual computer.” Somehow, it also became tied to the path of starting a company, and ended up becoming a vocation I created for myself. I am building Naia because I truly want to make this real. I am not simply trying to **make an AI chat app with a pretty avatar attached.** I am designing the structure in advance and researching it because, if Alpha can someday go beyond a virtual space and lead to a more physical form of AI, a physical AI, then I want to know what structure would be needed. That is **why Part 3, Chapter 6 talks about structuring it not as features, but in the form of a brain and cognitive structure**, and I am also developing related pieces whenever I can. Eyes that look at files and browsers, hands that execute tools, long-term memory, permission boundaries, voice, avatars, local execution environments, and interfaces that may later connect to physical devices all lead back to this question. But I decided that I could not present Alpha’s IP as-is for the public product. Alpha contains a lot of my tastes, personal stories, thoughts about family, and homages to works I have liked for a long time. Those are important to me, but they are too personal to present directly as a product brand to first-time users, and I do not intend to give them away. I heard that Vedal, the developer who created the AI YouTuber Neuro-sama, refused when someone offered to buy Neuro for a high price. I think it may be a similar kind of stubbornness. His attachment probably runs deeper than the software itself. Also, from a product planning standpoint, it leaned too heavily into a subculture aesthetic. On top of that, Naia uses a VRM avatar. Of course, I do not see that direction negatively. The early users are likely to be developers, AI tool users, and people interested in VTubers or character AI anyway, and many of them will already be familiar with that culture. But I judged that if even the product name and description pushed my personal IP directly, the entry barrier would become too high. So the public brand Naia needed a new character too. Naia is not a name that abandoned Alpha’s dream. It is a name that translates that dream into product language that more people can understand. If Alpha is a personal ideal and IP, Naia is the public brand that expresses that ideal as a visual shell, developer tools, local models, and an app ecosystem. ## 12.3 Naia’s Name and Character The first name I thought of was `NaN`. It is familiar to developers, short, and it also sounds a bit like a feminine name. But there was already a name called NaN OS, so it was hard to use as-is. I looked for another name that kept a similar feeling, and it became Naia. Naia carries several overlapping meanings. In the Greek-language world, Naiad evokes a water spirit. In the Basque-language world, Nahia connects to wind or wish. In Hawaiian, it also has the image of a dolphin. In Korean, it becomes a pun on “my AI.” As an English acronym, it can be read as Next-gen AI Agent. When greeting, it can also sound like “It’s me!” in Korean. It was not that I forced too many meanings into one name. I made and sorted many candidates with AI, and this name remained. The character design was also made together with AI. At first, because of the name, I thought of making it a water cat. Everyone knows the joke that cats are liquid. But then I thought about how humans are carbon-based life. I wanted to give the feeling that AI is not something completely separate from humans, but a being that works and lives together in the same world. So the character’s symbol shifted from water toward carbon. Of course, I am not trying to say that an actual liquid carbon character is scientifically possible. It is a design symbol. Carbon is the common basis of life, and when it hardens, it brings diamond to mind. The feeling of the character is not a scary T-1000 chasing you. It is closer to a Doraemon-like version of the T-1000. It changes form and creates the tools it needs, but it is not a being that threatens the user. It is a colleague that helps from beside you. Normally it appears transparent and soft, but when needed, it becomes solid. *Figure 12-4. Naia’s default character, “The Liquid Cat.” Based on the concept of a digital cat made of liquid carbon, it represents a colleague that normally flows transparently and becomes solid when needed.* ![Naia Character Variations](assets/naia/naia-variations.webp) *Figure 12-5. Naia character variations.* Personally, I also want to make USB drives containing naia-os and Naia stickers. They are not just merchandise. They are objects that give the feeling of holding “a workplace containing my AI” in your hand. Plugging in a USB drive with naia-os and booting from it, then putting a Naia sticker on a laptop or desktop, is not a feature in itself. But I think it matters quite a lot for how a project is remembered by people. ## 12.4 Why Go All the Way to an Operating System? If AI were only a tool that writes code, an IDE plugin or terminal tool might be enough. But if you want to treat AI like an actual colleague, the story changes. A colleague will not just look at code. They will look at issues, open browsers, read documents, leave work logs, check tool execution results, and ask the user for approval when needed. You can do some of this by putting a single app on top of an existing desktop environment. But as AI starts handling more and more tools, boundaries become necessary. You need standards for what files it can read, what commands it can execute, what memories it should leave, and what tasks require asking a human. Those standards are hard to finish with a few app settings. Naia looks at this problem from the perspective of a visual agent and AI OS structure. The user meets Naia through a character, dialogue box, voice, and apps, but internally the following layers move together. Here, it is more accurate to use `naia-os` narrowly as the name for the Bazzite/titanoboa-based custom distribution, rather than the name of the whole product. | Component | Role | Public Status | | --- | --- | --- | | `naia-shell` | The visual shell. It handles the character, dialogue box, browser, workspace UI, and app system. It is the surface the user directly meets, and it also handles flows for adding, modifying, and deleting apps. | Public | | `naia-agent` | The processing runtime that judges tasks, calls tools, and supervises external coding agents. It is close to Naia’s brain. | Public | | `naia-memory` | Handles long-term memory, user and project context, recall, and storage. It is the layer for leaving the time spent working together as the user’s asset. | Public | | `naia-adk` | The workspace format that contains storage structure, workplace rules, skills, and verification flows. It aims to be a structure that Claude Code, Codex, opencode, and naia-agent can all read together. | Public | | `naia-kb-compiler` | Compiles documents and materials into a structured knowledge base. It is the layer that attaches citations, governance, abstention, and answer-anchor verification so AI can answer with grounds. Knowledge settings live on the knowledge side, and the workspace is the surface for viewing and managing those knowledge files. | Public | | `naia-cognitive` | A research repo for multimodal cognitive and expressive capabilities such as voice, video avatars, singing, and expression models. | Private research | | `naia-video-avatar` | A public implementation repo for post-VRM video avatars, facial expressions, gaze, and lip sync. | Public | | `naia-omni-cascade` | A deployment-oriented multimodal cascade runtime that binds researched models and external models so they can be used in the product. It connects replaceable model adapters such as STT, LLM, TTS, voice, and video avatar formats like nva into real-time input and output flows. The current focus is real-time voice conversation and measuring latency and quality. | Private | | `naia-os` | A Bazzite/titanoboa-based custom distribution/ISO. It is the distribution layer that packages the stack above into a USB-bootable workplace. | Public | Seen this way, Naia is not a single program. The surface the user meets is a visual agent, and underneath it is an operating structure for AI to work. From a developer’s perspective, it is the work of building an entire AI work environment that loosely binds a shell, agent, memory, knowledge, skills, multimodal runtime, and distribution through contracts. Let me make one principle clear here. There are multiple layers, but **there is one judging core**. Anything about “what to do,” such as persona, workspace context, and shell/file tools, is owned by the brain core (`naia-agent`). The desktop shell (`naia-shell`) or command line (CLI) is only an environment and transport layer wrapping that core. Whether you meet it through the screen or the terminal, the same core answers. When a new entry point is added, the core logic is not copied. Only the transport is swapped. In practice, the CLI reuses the same core builder as gRPC. This applies the substrate-agnostic principle from Chapter 6 not only to the “body,” but also to the “entry points” where the user meets the AI. In particular, `naia-agent` is the actor inside Naia that codes and executes tools by itself, but I do not see it as a structure that must handle everything alone. It should also be able to collaborate with external coding AIs such as Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini. Naia aims to be a hub that places multiple AIs in the same workplace, records who did what, and ties them into a flow that a human can verify. ## 12.5 Why Bazzite? I had always wanted to use Linux as my main work OS. Because of that, I tried installing HamoniKR and even bought and used Zorin OS. Eventually, I arrived at Bazzite. Bazzite is known as a gaming Linux distribution, but the advantage I see is not only gaming. The important part is that it is an immutable OS. An immutable OS does not let the system’s core areas be changed freely in the usual way. Updates are managed by image, and if something goes wrong, it is easy to roll back to a previous state. In an era where AI executes tools and touches development environments, this stability matters. We cannot trust AI to always judge everything correctly. The system should not break easily, and even if it breaks, it should be recoverable. Another reason is GPU and gaming environments. Many of the powerful GPUs owned by individuals are inside gaming PCs. Consumer GPUs such as RTX 3090, 4090, and 5090 can run games and also local AI models. Bazzite fits this environment well. It preserves a gaming environment including Steam, while also making it convenient to use containers and development tools. I now feel much less need for a few specific Windows apps. If I need something, I can build it myself with vibe coding, and most work can be replaced well enough with open-source apps. Writing documents, browsing, code editing, terminal work, media tools, and container-based development are all sufficiently possible on Linux. On top of that, there is the advantage of being able to customize the OS itself. From a commercial perspective, a Bazzite-based custom ISO also has meaning. naia-os can be put on a USB drive and booted. You can carry the user’s AI workplace around even without an internal SSD or HDD. The same Naia environment can be launched on a temporary company PC, educational equipment, or a personal gaming PC. Of course, in real operation, more problems need to be solved, including security, licensing, device authentication, and storage separation. But the direction is clear. The naia-os distribution is closer to a bootable workplace containing my AI than a single installable app. ![Naia Desktop App Running](assets/en/plug-usb-and-run-ai.webp) *Figure 12-6. An OS that can also be booted and run from USB.* ## 12.6 What Naia Provides If you look at Naia only as a feature list, it can be divided into items such as avatar, chat, browser, apps, local models, memory, and reports. But the core is “an environment for working with AI.” First, Naia provides a face for talking with AI. It is not just text chat. It is an interface where a 3D VRM avatar, voice, facial expressions, gaze, and work status are visible together. The user should be able to see whether the AI is listening, speaking, thinking, or executing a tool. This also includes features for users to customize their own work environment. They can change the VRM avatar, change the wallpaper, and play MP3 files or YouTube music. This is not just decoration. If an AI is going to stay on all day and work together with the user, the atmosphere and work rhythm the user finds comfortable matter. I see Naia not as a window where you throw commands, but as a work environment the user can customize to their taste and stay in for a long time. ![Naia Playing Music by Voice](assets/en/naia-music-en.webp) *Figure 12-7. The Naia app playing music by voice. Beyond text chat, a 3D avatar can perform conversation and work.* Second, Naia provides tools for AI to actually work. The browser, workspace, file explorer, terminal, and app system play that role. Apps are not a separate layer, but a way to extend the work environment inside `naia-shell`. The Naia shell needs to provide flows for adding apps, fixing settings and configuration, and deleting apps that are no longer needed. For AI to open a browser on behalf of a person, read materials, and edit files, it needs software equivalent to eyes and hands. The workspace can view, search, modify, delete, and save files in the work area. It includes a Markdown viewer that renders Mermaid, PDF and image viewers, and Git integration. It was also made so that documents that are hard to inspect from the CLI can be checked easily when working with AI. ![Naia workspace dashboard](assets/en/workspace-dashboard-en.webp) *Figure 12-8. Naia workspace for working with AI. It is still quite unstable. For now, the most useful parts are probably the Markdown viewer and PDF printing that includes Mermaid.* Third, Naia makes it possible to use local models and cloud models together. This does not mean solving everything only locally, nor does it mean handing everything over to the cloud. Depending on cost, performance, privacy, and hardware conditions, they can be mixed appropriately. `naia-omni-cascade`, covered in Chapter 13, and the omni model profiles inside it are one example of this axis. Users can choose how to run models according to their hardware situation, and I consider this axis important because I ultimately want to build my own AI that fits my own local environment. ![Naia model settings](assets/en/model-select-en.webp) *Figure 12-9. Naia model settings. In addition to Naia’s own account, it supports various APIs and ollama and vllm as interfaces for local LLMs.* Fourth, Naia works in a direction where memory and records remain under the user’s ownership. It creates work context that remains on the user’s project and device side, rather than records that briefly stay inside a cloud service and disappear. This is why Naia uses the phrase “my AI.” Naia Memory, which handles this memory, and the knowledge compiler (`naia-kb-compiler`) for grounded answers already appear in the layer table in 12.4. The structure modeled after human memory, and the method of compiling knowledge from source folders and citing it as evidence, are covered separately in Chapter 14. Fifth, Naia has an app ecosystem. The browser and workspace are included as default apps, and features such as content studio, issue management, education, and music are extended as apps. Instead of fixing every feature into the `naia-shell` core, additional apps are left open so anyone can directly make, register, modify, and delete them. How to develop apps and attach them to the shell is explained separately in Chapter 15. ## 12.7 What Makes Naia Different — Compared with OpenClaw, Hermes, and Claude Code Naia is not the only tool moving in this direction. Many products already exist under names like AI desktop, AI colleague, and coding agent. So there is a question I often receive, and one I also keep thinking about: “How is it different from what already exists?” To be honest up front, Naia is not a product that tries to beat those tools on one-line specs. It is closer to an attempt to move the axis of comparison itself. I will explain by using three representative comparison targets. **Claude Code — absorption, not competition.** Coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini are strong at writing code inside terminals and editors. Naia is not trying to make yet another coding CLI in the same position. Instead, it tries to place them as subagents inside the workplace (12.4). Naia’s axis is not code itself, but the way AI is present in front of the user: face (avatar), voice, workplace (environment), and memory. Coding is delegated to external coding AIs inside that workplace, and Naia acts as a hub that records who did what and ties it into a flow a person can verify. So Claude Code is closer to a tool that Naia places and uses inside itself than a competitor. I want Naia to become a work coordinator or a friend who gives reports. I want to make it a good team lead and assistant more than a genius developer. **Hermes — less a comparison, more that I am going my own way.** To be honest, I am not a user who has used Hermes long enough. So it would not be right to say here, “this is better than Hermes.” But it does seem clear that recent AI colleague tools are moving toward reviewing conversations, remembering user preferences or repeated instructions, and reflecting them in the next task. Naia also considers that direction important. I can take what is good, and build what I want to build. In fact, Naia periodically evaluates other open-source AI tools and continues to absorb structures or features worth bringing in. The self-improvement loop seen in Hermes is one of them, and some of it has already been brought into Naia’s workflow and applied. Chapter 14 covers in detail what that first work was and how it was brought in safely. What I want to focus on more in Naia is where that feature is placed. Memory should not live only inside a cloud service, but remain as much as possible on the user’s device and repository side. AI should not be only a chat window or one work tool, but should stand inside a personal workplace with an avatar, voice, work status, apps, and a local execution environment. So this section is less a comparison with a competing product and more an explanation of where the problem I want to solve with Naia sits. **OpenClaw — the starting point, and beyond it.** Naia started from a Windows version of OpenClaw (12.1). But it did not stop there. Naia adds three main things. The first is the separation of brain, body, and environment. Cognition (the brain) is kept from being tied to a specific device, and the body (avatar and voice) and environment (workplace and tools) are designed to be swappable. That way, if it someday moves beyond the desktop into physical devices, the brain does not have to be rebuilt (12.2). The second is an ecosystem divided into four repos (12.4). Shell, agent, memory, and workplace interlock only through contracts. The third is local model serving and the direction of keeping memory under user ownership. **Naia is an attempt to expand “AI as a work tool” into a user-owned workplace, local execution environment, and memory structure.** It is not just a tool that codes well, a colleague that remembers only through text, or an assistant that lives only in the cloud. Many of these differentiators are still being built. Some actually work, and some are still closer to skeletons. The state we guard against most is “many skeletons, but few things that actually turn on.” So before adding more new features, we try to keep the discipline of turning on and operating the structures we have already built. This includes standards such as whether the body and environment work even without a brain, and whether we distinguish between tests being green and the thing actually turning on. The contracts, structure, traceability, and verification discussed throughout this book are tested most harshly in Naia right here. ## 12.8 Workspace: The Desk Where AI Works In Naia, the workspace is not yet a finished feature. It is closer to a core concept that shows what kind of workplace Naia is aiming for. The goal is not just to attach a simple file explorer or code editor. For AI to actually work, it needs to see files, documents, knowledge, running tasks, and the status of subagents in one place. Just as files, notes, colleagues, and reference materials sit together on a human desk, the workspace is a space where AI and humans share the same workplace. A workspace explorer, Obsidian-like knowledge notes, and subagent management sit together inside it. However, the settings and compilation flow for knowledge management itself are the responsibility of `naia-kb-compiler` and the knowledge layer. The workspace is closer to a file management surface that lets humans see, fix, connect, and attach those knowledge sources and output files to work. The concrete shape of each axis and how to use it as an app are covered separately in Chapter 15. It is not all finished yet, but it is the part that most clearly shows why Naia must be a workplace, not just an avatar app. ## 12.9 Why Operate Open Source Primarily in Korean? The new version of Naia intends to operate open source primarily in Korean. This does not mean we will not write English documents. Code, README files, manuals, and release notes obviously need to be provided in English and other languages as well. It means that decisions, issue organization, design discussions, and the source of truth for operating standards will not be kept only in English from the beginning. As development with AI has accelerated, the amount a small number of developers can do has increased greatly. Work that used to require many people for a long time can now be quickly experimented on and implemented by one or two people with AI. In this structure, decision-making needs to be simple. Core ideas need to be shared quickly, fixed quickly, and verified quickly. In the past, I participated in a Mozilla developer event with XRCloud, a B2B version of Mozilla Hubs. It was a good experience, but the barriers of language and time zones were larger than I expected. Reading code and making PRs is different from following community discussions and aligning direction. Even when people are well-intentioned toward each other, collaboration can slow down, and even a small decision can take a long time. So Naia sees Korean developers and Korean-language operations as one form of competitiveness. We discuss accurately in Korean first, then expand that content through AI translation and multilingual documentation. We do not feel ashamed of Korean issues and PRs. Instead, we have AI translate and organize them into forms that external contributors can read. Korean-centered operations and multilingual public release are treated as separate concerns. This is also connected to Naia’s AI-native open-source experiment. It is not a structure where many people slowly reach consensus, but one where a small number of people build quickly with AI, and open the necessary points to the outside through documents, translation, and verification. The goal is not to imitate English-speaking communities. The goal is to keep the language in which we actually think and decide as the source of truth, and to experiment with an open-source operation that connects outward through AI. ## 12.10 Public Repos Where You Can Participate Now Naia is not a project meant only to be watched. We want development participation. But mixing public status and participation targets becomes confusing. The table in 12.4 is the standard for public status. Here, I list the work you can participate in right away from repositories currently confirmed as public. | Public Repo | Work You Can Participate In | | --- | --- | | `naia-shell` | Tauri, React, visual shell, browser integration, workspace UI, app system, app add/modify/delete flows | | `naia-agent` | Tool calls, task judgment, external coding agent integration, work logs, permission and verification flows | | `naia-memory` | Long-term memory, user and project context, recall and storage policy, local memory store | | `naia-kb-compiler` | Document collection, structuring, answer-anchor verification, citation and governance, knowledge file management and compilation flow | | `naia-adk` | AGENTS rules, documents, verification system, new project templates | | `naia-video-avatar` | Post-VRM video avatars, facial expressions, gaze, and lip sync | | `naia-os` | Bazzite/titanoboa-based distribution, ISO builds, packaging a bootable AI workplace | There are also common contribution areas that are not tied to a single repo. | Common Contribution | Work You Can Participate In | | --- | --- | | Documentation and translation | Installation documents, developer manuals, Korean and English, multilingual translation review | | Testing and operations | E2E tests, cost measurement, issue reports, integration of automated verification results | `naia-content-studio`, `naia-omni-cascade`, and `naia-omni-windows-manager` are currently private repos. So they are omitted from the table of public repos you can participate in now, and their direction and structure are explained as needed in later chapters. Small contributions also matter. Filling gaps in installation documents, making one app, organizing local model execution logs, reproducing a place where Windows gets stuck, and improving Korean sentences so they are easier to read are all needed. What matters in open source in the AI era is not necessarily completing a huge feature alone. It is sending back to the project the grounds that a human has seen and judged. ## 12.11 The Meaning of Paid Subscriptions and Sponsorship We also need to talk realistically. Naia is both a personal project and a company project. Model API costs, server costs, authentication and payments, deployment, test equipment, and local GPU environments all require money and time. So Naia has both paid subscriptions and GitHub sponsorship. A subscription is product access, but it is also a way to buy development time. To keep building stable releases, better documentation, local model integration, an app ecosystem, a memory system, and agent work reports, a sustainable cost structure is needed. However, the reason I mention subscriptions in this chapter is not to ask you to believe in and buy a completed product. At this stage, it is closer to sponsorship. It is a request to participate if you agree with the direction Naia is taking: a direction where individuals have their own AI, and developers directly own the workplace where they work with AI. ## 12.12 What to Take Away from This Chapter Naia is not a completed answer. It is an experimental ground for turning the problems discussed in this book into an actual project. It is a project for checking whether AI can stop remaining only as a cloud session that newly appears every time, and instead settle into the user’s workplace, memory, tools, and relationships. For users, I want to provide the experience of having their own AI. For developers, I want to provide an opportunity to directly fix and extend a workplace where they work with AI. In the open-source ecosystem, I want to experiment with whether AI can become not simply a being that takes and uses code, but a member that returns documents, issues, verification, and contributions back to the project. The next chapter separately covers the local model axis, especially `naia-omni-cascade` and the omni model profiles inside it. If Naia is a visual agent, this axis is the part that gives that agent a voice and multimodal execution capability.
