Yujin heard the words. They were the same boats. Only the name had changed.

Two AH-64Fs came in late, flying low along the coastline. The sound of their rotors seemed to press down on the entire sky. The helicopters were far louder than they appeared on the screen. As they flew low, their rotor wash lifted dust from the ridge, and small stones struck Yujin’s protective suit. The orcs’ small boats seemed to shudder even at a distance beyond the reach of the wind. The sound alone was weapon enough.

The helicopter pilot requested permission to pursue the refugee boats. Hale did not answer for a moment. Supplies, fuel, rules of engagement, video records, the possibility of civilians. Everything was on a single screen. None of it offered him absolution.

“Confirm wreckage of the large vessel. For the smaller craft, tracking markers only for now.”

That was what he said.

Menon closed his eyes. Yujin could not tell whether it was relief or despair. The Black Ship sank slowly. A piece of burning sail floated on the water. One oar seemed to keep moving, but then a wave turned it over. The landing craft’s turret followed the wreckage, then stopped. There was nothing left to shoot.

Menon whispered, “They succeeded.”

Yujin looked at him.

“Who did?”

Menon did not answer. If he did, the answer would remain on the Earth forces’ radio network. If it remained, it would be erased.

The landing craft tried to reestablish the coastal blockade. But most of the refugee boats had already scattered. The Inland Sea was wide, and the small boats dwindled on the thermal display. The time the Black Ship had bought was not long. But in war, a few minutes could be long enough. A few minutes were enough for a child to crawl beneath a boat, for an old man to hide under a sail, for a group to pass beyond the tracking line.

Hale submitted the end-of-operation report.

Large enemy vessel sunk. Minor damage to Landing Craft One’s external sensor. Tracking lost on multiple refugee boats.

The words refugee boats appeared briefly, then were changed to local vessels in the final report.

Yujin’s camera retained the words from before the change. He did not know what that would mean later. Records often failed to change the world. Even so, what went unrecorded died sooner.

When night fell, the Inland Sea grew dark again. An oily stain and charred pieces of wood floated where the Black Ship had been. Far away, very far away, small sails vanished below the red horizon.

The Earth forces recorded another victory that day.

chapters.title: 18. Mars Underfoot
chapters.markdown:
# 18. Mars Underfoot

![Chapter 18 Illustration](resources/assets/chapter-18.webp)

The day after the naval battle, the tank did not look at the sea.

A lone Abrams stood on a low hill outside the Citadel Belt. Its gun pointed west, but the auxiliary antenna at the rear of the hull tilted toward the patch of sky where the orbiter would pass. The engine was off to conserve fuel. The tank could move, but it did not. Movement meant burning fuel, and the fuel had come from Earth.

Yujin passed beside it without touching the hull. The metal looked cold even in daylight. A tanker was checking the orbital satellite's pass time. He glanced at his wrist terminal, then brushed the red dust from the hull with a gloved hand. Dust settled again on the spot he had cleared.

“You're only looking at the sky,” Yujin said.

The tanker gave a weary smile.

“Because that's where the food is.”

There really were supplies in the sky. The orbiter's cargo holds carried medicine and food, batteries, relays, and spare filters. The problem was getting them down. Orbit to the landing zone was possible. The stretch from the landing zone to the front was the problem. On the map, it was a short line. In reality, it was a road through the Red Forest and gorges, past burned-out relays, through fog and the sound of orc war horns.

Other soldiers were working in the maintenance tent beside the tank. They cleaned the gun barrel, removed filters, and scraped dust from between the armor plates. The tank looked like a symbol of war, but in truth it was a mass of endless maintenance. Fire the gun, and the heat had to be bled off. Move, and the tracks had to be checked. Even standing still, dust found its way inside. Someone calculated fuel. Someone rationed lubricant. Someone numbered the little boxes so the spare bolts would not go missing.

Yujin filmed the scene for a long time. Viewers on Earth usually wanted launches and explosions. But what soldiers actually did most was clean, tighten, carry, and wait.

Hale's temporary command post occupied a room on the outskirts of the Citadel Belt. The paintings on the walls had been covered with cloth. The Earth forces had done that. An operations map was pinned over them. A room in the Citadel Belt had become a conference room, and the red powder left on the floor was no longer dust from someone's home but a potentially contaminated substance.

Nowak pointed to the Southern Gorge supply route.

“The forward mobile detachment has made it this far. We can sustain it with two relays, provided we restore Number Five.”

“Five died yesterday,” Hale said.

“Then we need to put up a replacement.”

“Heliborne?” Major Lukas Weber shook his head. He commanded the heliborne company. He had short blond hair and always spoke quietly. The quietness sounded less like confidence than exhaustion.

“We can fly. Landing is the problem. The air currents inside the gorge are unstable, and there are no landing markers. The terrain data is also wrong after yesterday's storm. The AH-64F can go in and scare them. The UH-60V has to land and take people aboard. Those are two different things.”

“Drone drops.”

“Possible. Not precise.”

The conference room fell silent. Possible and precise were not the same thing. In war, the difference was measured in people. A cargo drone could drop around forty kilograms. One crate of medicine, one bundle of batteries, part of an ammunition load. But the numbers did not add up when it came to feeding seventy-three people at the front three times a day, sheltering the wounded, repairing relays, and keeping the guns and robots moving.

“The orbiter has ample food remaining,” Vosrov said from the screen.

Nowak answered at once.

“If it's on the orbiter, it isn't at the front.”

There was no insolence in the remark. It was physics.

Captain Han Doyun's forward company was already at the mouth of the gorge. They had been ordered to pursue the retreating bands of orcs after the Black Ship incident while also securing the southern relay and landing markers. On the map, both missions pointed in the same direction. In reality, they were different. Pursuit meant moving forward. Securing supply lines meant protecting the connection behind them. One unit could not be responsible for both directions at once.

Yujin listened to the forward company's channel.

“Supply Vehicle Two, slow down.”

It was Captain Han Doyun's voice.

“Condition of the bridge ahead unknown.”

“We checked it with the drone.”

“The drone looked from above. It didn't put wheels on it.”

A moment later, the bridge appeared on the screen. It was a narrow bridge built of red timber and stone. A medieval bridge. Too weak for an armored vehicle. A person could cross it, and a cart probably could have as well. The Earth forces' Boxer armored vehicle was too heavy. In coming to Mars, the Earth forces had brought an age more advanced than their enemy's. But they had brought the weight of that advanced age with them.

“Go around,” Captain Han Doyun said.

There was no alternate route on the map. The drone would have to find one. Meanwhile, the sun sank lower, and the delay between the front and the landing zone grew. Something like a red bird flew above the gorge. No one could tell whether it was a bird or a bat. The tactical network marked it as nonthreatening fauna. A moment later, the relay signal beneath it dropped by one bar.

“Did something pass by?”

“Checking.”

“Don't just look up. Look down too.”

Captain Han Doyun's words cut out, then resumed. The signal was unstable.

Yujin looked through the command post window. Several carts abandoned by the orcs stood outside the Citadel Belt. One was loaded with small water vessels. The Earth forces had marked them off-limits pending analysis. Even the thirsty soldiers did not drink the water. For now, the rules still held.

Menon was looking at the cart.

“They left their water behind because of us,” Nowak spoke.

“We can't use that water.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

Menon did not answer. The same vessels held abandoned property for some and unusable danger for others. And in a few days, they might mean something else again. Yujin could not shake the thought. Water, roots, meat, corpses. War advanced by changing the names of things.

Night fell, and the orbiter passed overhead. A single point of light moved slowly across the sky. A few soldiers raised their heads. Everyone knew it held food, medicine, and spare parts. The point brightened, then dimmed. While it passed, it looked like hope. After it was gone, it looked like a greater distance.

Captain Han Doyun's voice came over the forward channel again.

“Reached gorge entrance. Relay status unstable. Will attempt to restore Number Five tomorrow.”

Hale gave a brief reply.

“Don't push too hard.”

Captain Han Doyun was silent for a moment.

“If we don't, there was no point in coming this far.” It was not insubordination. The whole Earth force was already operating by the same logic. A little farther, and we will be safe. Change a little more, and we can survive. Push a little harder, and we will gain new land. They must have said the same thing as Earth was breaking.

chapters.title: 19. The Ruined Supply Route
chapters.markdown:
# 19. The Ruined Supply Route

![Chapter 19 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-19.webp)

A cargo drone was burning on the canyon floor.

One wing was caught on a rock, and the other had folded into a blackened mass. Beneath the drone’s belly lay three crates of medical supplies and one crate of ammunition. There were no food crates. There had never been any. This drop was for repairing the relay and treating the wounded. Food was coming on the next drop.

At the front, next was becoming a worse word by the day.

Captain Han Doyun studied the drone for a long moment, then nudged the scorched wing with his boot. It broke easily. Fragments of carbon fiber fell onto the red mud. He did not step on them again. Even the smallest piece might prove useful later. The longer a war lasts, the harder it becomes to tell trash from spare parts.

“Were the landing coordinates correct?”

“The coordinates were correct,” the signalman spoke.

“The signal jumped in the last forty meters. One of the landing markers disappeared, and the aircraft tried to avoid an obstacle automatically and hit the rock—”

“Why did it disappear?”

The signalman could not answer.

Kenji picked up a broken piece of the marker from the ground. The metal rod was bent, and a red cord had been tied to its end. It was not decoration. It looked as though someone had deliberately pulled it out and marked it. The orcs might not have understood what the marker meant. But they had learned that it summoned metal from the sky.

“They’ve learned,” Kenji spoke.

“Where the drones come down.”

Captain Han Doyun nodded. It was no surprise. Earth’s forces were learning the orcs’ roads and signals as well. The enemy had simply learned too. The problem was how slow Earth’s forces had been to admit that the enemy could learn. Superstitious response, incidental destruction, instinctive avoidance. The language of the reports kept postponing the fact that the enemy could think.

Two quadruped supply robots made their way down toward the drone wreckage. One loaded a crate of medical supplies, while the other secured the ammunition. The third robot could not come. It had stopped at the canyon entrance with a joint warning. Two mechanics worked on it, but the spare parts were at the landing zone.

“Do we leave the robot behind?” the squad leader asked.

Kenji answered at once.

“After we strip it for parts.”

“We don’t have time.”

“Without those parts, we won’t have the next robot either.”

Captain Han Doyun looked at them both.

“Essential parts only. Five minutes.”

Five minutes stretched. The screws were caked with dirt, their hands were wet, and the powered suit batteries had fallen below half charge. Kenji knelt and removed a small motor and a sensor module. He packed them more carefully than the ammunition. A bullet vanished when fired, but one sensor could find the road again and again.

The canyon was narrow. Seen from above, it was a simple valley, but once inside it, the walls cut away the sky. Red moss and black vines clung to cracks in the rock, and somewhere water could be heard running. The road the orcs used had been made for people and carts. Earth’s armored vehicles and robots, powered suits and stretchers had to keep widening it. Widening it made noise, and whenever there was noise, movement began above the canyon.

A Black Hawk made one approach, then turned back. Its sound was low and immense. The beating rotors struck the canyon walls and came back from several directions. When the downdraft descended, red dust and leaves rose all at once. One soldier instinctively ducked. The helicopter looked like a symbol of rescue, but up close it became fear first. Running with a stretcher in that wind was nearly impossible.

“Unable to land.”

Weber’s voice came over the radio.

“Unstable airflow. Insufficient fuel reserve. If we make another approach, we won’t make it back.”

Captain Han Doyun looked up at the sky. The helicopter was nowhere in sight. Only the sound remained, then faded. After it was gone, the silence felt deeper. The soldiers hated that silence. At least the noise of the helicopter was proof that someone was looking for them.

“Did you hear that?” he spoke.

“Yes, sir.”

“Then we walk out.”

“What about the wounded?”

The question remained in the canyon.

There were eight wounded. Three could walk, four needed stretchers, and one was slipping in and out of consciousness. Two armored vehicles were still operational, but they were low on fuel, and the road out of the canyon was narrow. They had taken a detour because they could not cross the bridge, and they would have to take the same detour back. The robots could pull the stretchers, but pulling them required batteries. The drone had brought the batteries, and the drone had crashed.

Communications quality was at two bars. The orbiter was watching them. Vosrov enlarged the blue dots of the forward company on her display. Seo Yujin also watched those dots through the orbital relay feed. The blue dots were still moving. On the display, the forward company looked small and orderly. In reality, every person carried a different smell, different blood, different complaints, and different fear.

Nowak’s calculations appeared on the command network.

Forward detachment food remaining: 42 hours. 36 hours with priority allocation to the wounded. Probability of recovery: low until weather and fuel conditions improve and relay service is restored.

The numbers were coldly precise. That made them crueler. The number thirty-six hours did not explain hunger. It did not explain the feeling of the stomach hollowing out, the chill in the fingertips, or the moment everyone turned at the sound of someone tearing open a ration pack.

An orc horn sounded above the canyon. This time it was close. The soldiers raised their rifles. The forest was out of sight. There was only movement among the red leaves and rocks above the canyon. One soldier magnified the thermal image. The points scattered quickly.

The first stone landed beside the communications antenna. A strip of burning cloth was tied to the second. It landed far from the ammunition crate, but close to the sunshade. A soldier grabbed a fire extinguisher and ran. As he ran, a short spear dropped from above. It struck his shoulder plate and glanced away. The plate held, but the impact knocked him down.

The M250A1 roared. A short burst. The rounds tore through the red leaves above the canyon and sparked against the rock. An orc tumbled down. His body struck a rock once on the way and came to rest beside the drone wreckage. No one approached. Everyone saw him, and everyone pretended to look elsewhere.

Captain Han Doyun took the radio.

“Landing zone, this is Forward. Relay Five repair failed. Cargo drone down. Eight wounded. Switching to the thirty-six-hour food schedule.”

Hale’s reply came after a brief delay.

“Forward, hold your position. We’re preparing the next drop.”

“Food?”

Silence.

“Medical supplies and batteries take priority.”

Captain Han Doyun did not close his eyes. He ran through the names of those still alive on the screen. Beside each name were heart rate, oxygen saturation, ammunition, and remaining battery charge. People had become numbers, and the numbers were still alive.

“Understood,” he spoke.

Something moved again above the canyon. A soldier fired. The gunshot struck the canyon and came back. The sound was too loud and lingered too long.

Before nightfall, they covered the dead orc’s body with cloth. The record did not say who first suggested it. Menon later saw it and stood there for a long time. Dubois ordered everyone to keep away. Ben Youssef reduced the remaining doses of painkillers for the wounded.

Food was coming on the next drop.

chapters.title: 20. Days Trapped
chapters.markdown:
# 20. Days Trapped

![Chapter 20 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-20.webp)

The roof of the field tent kept out the rain, but not the sound.

The wounded moaned through the night. Some softly, others holding it in until an occasional cry broke loose. Mixed with the rain striking the tent, it was hard to tell human sounds from water. Major Sara Ben Youssef gave up trying. She watched the vital signs instead: oxygen saturation, blood pressure, body temperature, remaining pain medication.

Seo Yujin sat in a corner of the tent, charging his last battery. The charger was connected to a backup power supply salvaged from a quadruped robot. The current was weak, and the screen kept dimming. He did not turn off the camera. If he turned it off now, there was no knowing what might be gone when he switched it back on. On a battlefield, the charge left in a battery was also the measure of memory remaining.

Dubois marked the entrance to the tent with quarantine tape. It was red.

“We eat in here, treat patients in here, and dispose of waste in here.”

Captain Han Doyun asked,

“Do we have anything to eat?”

Dubois did not answer. She preferred questions she could answer. The worst situation for the person in charge of quarantine was not having no answer, but knowing the answer and lacking the power to make people comply.

The remaining food looked even scarcer laid out in full. Three nutrition packs for the wounded, twelve compressed emergency rations, a few glucose gels, electrolyte supplements, and flavorless protein bars. Divided among seventy-three people, it was not food but procedure. Paperwork deciding who ate first, who ate half, and who drank only water.

Nowak’s calculations came down again.

Wounded first. Maintain minimum combat strength. Strict water rationing. Thirty-six hours.

“And after thirty-six hours?” Yujin asked.

Captain Han Doyun did not look up from the food inventory.

“We’ll get a different number.”

“A rescue estimate?”

“Or a death toll.”

His words were dry. Yujin did not think him cruel. They were not cruel words, only words wrung dry of moisture.

Outside the tent, squads began reporting their remaining ammunition again. As the quartermaster called out quantities, the soldiers searched their combat uniform pockets and the floors of armored vehicles to make the numbers match. Some squads started counting over from the beginning when they came up one round short. Spare batteries for the powered suits went first to the sentries and casualty teams. Everyone else had to shut off power assist and walk. All drone batteries not needed for reconnaissance were diverted to the relay. Since becoming trapped in the gorge, the names of their equipment no longer mattered. Only the time remaining did.

Menon was crouched outside the tent. A short distance away, a dead orc lay covered with cloth. The body had tumbled down into the gorge during the fighting. At first no one noticed it. Later, everyone tried not to look.

Yujin sat beside Menon.

“Did you cover it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Menon looked at the end of the wet cloth.

“They did the same.”

One foot protruded slightly from beneath the cloth. It was easy to see why someone had compared it to a pig’s hoof. The ease of the resemblance made it more disturbing. There had been jokes when Earth’s forces first classified the orcs. Boars, muscle pigs, pigs in armor. The words had come out of tension and raised laughter, and the laughter had seemed to keep people alive. But now the foot beneath the cloth carried those jokes somewhere else.

“Some people are thinking about that,” Yujin said.

Menon nodded.

“I know.”

“Can you stop them?”

“I have no command authority.”

“You can still say something.”

Menon looked at Yujin.

“I already am.”

That, too, was true. And it was not enough.

As night deepened, orc movement was detected again above the gorge. They did not attack at once. Small groups appeared and vanished, and from time to time stones or burning cloth fell. Earth’s forces returned fire. The gunshots rang loudly, and the ammunition dwindled. Heavy weapons were too loud inside the gorge. A few seconds of fire from an M240L made the rocks tremble, and the insides of people’s chests trembled with them.

Sergeant Nakamura Kenji swallowed a curse as he changed the barrel.

“If we keep firing this thing, the gun and the people will both give out first.”

“How much do we have left?” Captain Han Doyun asked.

“The barrel, the ammunition, or the people?”

No one laughed.

Near dawn, a reply came from the orbiter. Preparing next drop. Awaiting weather clearance. Food supplies under consideration.

Under consideration.

Yujin looked at the words and checked his remaining battery. Seventeen percent.

Inside the tent, one of the wounded moaned again. Captain Han Doyun stood for a long time, listening. Outside, the rain showed no sign of stopping. The cloth-covered body of the orc lay in the rain.

By morning, the soldiers spoke less. Hunger made jokes at first, then irritation, and then silence. Whenever someone folded the wrapper from a ration pack, several people turned to look at once. Ben Youssef squeezed glucose gel into a wounded patient’s mouth and tried to keep her hands from trembling. Dubois printed the prohibition against consuming local organisms again. The paper grew wet, its edges curling.

“That regulation was written for peacetime,” someone said.

Dubois looked up.

“Quarantine does not distinguish between peace and war.”

“Not even after we’re dead?” the soldier who had asked the question quickly looked away. His face showed that he had realized where his words had led.

Captain Han Doyun said nothing. He went outside the tent and looked at the orc’s cloth-covered body. The rain had made the cloth heavy. He stood before it for a long time. Orders always seemed to come later than people, but in truth they first took shape in the mind. By the time they were spoken aloud, what they set in motion had already begun long before.

No one had drawn a knife yet.

chapters.title: 21. A Council That Eats the Dead
chapters.markdown:
# 21. A Council That Eats the Dead

![Chapter 21 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-21.webp)


Rainwater had pooled at the edge of the cloth covering the dead orc.

The water was undrinkable. The cloth was not to be touched. Dubois had said so. Gloves, masks, cutting tools, waste bags, decontamination procedures. Her words were precise, and seemed useless in equal measure. Procedure was too flimsy in the face of hunger. But flimsy did not mean it could be torn aside. Dubois knew that. Knowing it only made her angrier.

Captain Han Doyun convened a meeting inside the armored vehicle. It was too cramped to call a meeting. He stood, Ben Youssef held the casualty list, and Dubois clenched both hands into fists to keep from folding her arms. Menon stood by the door. Yujin had not been granted permission to film. Instead, he switched on his recorder. It was unclear whether he had permission to record, either. But Han Doyun did not send him out.

The armored vehicle smelled of wet metal and human sweat. The screen on the wall kept flickering. It alternated between the forward company’s vital signs and supply charts. People with racing hearts, people with low body temperatures, people who needed painkillers, people for whom there was nothing left to give. The numbers beside their names bore down on the meeting.

“Consumption of local organisms is prohibited,” Dubois spoke.

“I know,” Han Doyun answered.

“No. Saying you know isn’t enough. Bodily fluids, organs, muscle, bone marrow—they’re all dangerous. We don’t even have standards for heat treatment. We don’t know whether they’re toxic or infectious. We know nothing about their protein structures, symbionts, or parasites. You’re proposing that we eat what we do not understand.”

“That’s why preparation will be restricted.”

“That phrase is scientifically meaningless.”

Dubois raised her voice for the first time.

“This isn’t a choice between dying from a small amount and dying from a large one. We must not eat them.”

Ben Youssef looked down at the list.

“Three of the wounded are unlikely to survive the night. We’re out of nutrition packs.”

“Feeding them this could kill them faster.”

“Not feeding them will certainly kill them.” Ben Youssef brought up another display. It showed records from the animals used for biometric monitoring that had gone missing during the fighting. A drone had captured footage of one dog and two cats that had fled beyond the landing zone tearing flesh from orcs killed after the battle in the gorge. All three were still alive. Neither their body temperatures nor their gait had deteriorated significantly. The data did not constitute a safety test. Dubois said so. But to starving people, it looked like evidence.

The armored vehicle fell silent. Only the rain striking the hull could be heard. It was quieter than the night before, but sounded louder inside.

Menon spoke.

“They are a sentient species.”

Han Doyun looked at him.

“I know.”

“They are fallen soldiers. Bodies. Not potential food.”

“I know that too.”

“And you still intend to do this?”

Han Doyun did not answer at once. He looked at the list of those who remained on the screen. Beside each name were vital signs, ammunition, battery charge, and injury classification. Some could still carry a rifle. Some could no longer swallow water. One had only closed his eyes for a moment, yet his heart rate had dropped on the screen.

“Something similar happened during the Korean Civil War.”

No one inside the armored vehicle moved.

“We were cut off in an underground position in the northern mountains. The passage collapsed. No supplies came. No rescue came. In the end, the only thing separating the dead from the living was a name tag.”

Menon watched Han Doyun’s face. Han Doyun did not look away.

“The dead weren’t even the enemy that time. They were my comrades.”

He did not say how much they had eaten, or who had first picked up the knife. He did not need to. Everyone inside the armored vehicle understood.

“And that means you can do it again?”

“I’m not saying I can.”

Han Doyun looked at the list again.

“I’m saying I know what kind of order I’m giving.”

“I have to get these people out of here,” he spoke.

“Does that settle everything?” Menon asked.

“No.”

Han Doyun shook his head.

“That’s why I’m putting it on record. Order for restricted preparation. Responsible officer: Han Doyun.”

Yujin checked that the recorder was running. His hand trembled slightly.

Dubois stepped forward.

“Putting your responsibility in writing doesn’t change the biology.”

“I know.”

“No. Captain, you’re pretending to take responsibility while ignoring the warning.”

The air inside the armored vehicle changed. Ben Youssef looked at Dubois, and Han Doyun’s eyelids shifted almost imperceptibly.

“I’m not pretending,” he spoke.

“Then that’s worse.”

Dubois pointed at the screen.

“Because of those numbers, you’re going to create others. Numbers of infected, exposed, and dead. Right now, we have to say we don’t know. We have to stop because we don’t know.”

“I can’t let them die because we don’t know.”

“And you can’t kill everyone because we don’t know.”

At that moment, the radio cut in. A surveillance drone above the gorge had detected brief movement. Everyone looked at the screen. Several orcs were approaching from a distance, trying to recover the bodies. They were armed, but did not attack immediately. One carried a long strip of torn cloth. It bore a twist resembling a funerary marker.

Menon’s face hardened.

“They’ve come for the bodies,” the squad leader asked.

“Do we block their approach?”

Han Doyun did not answer for several seconds.

“Block them. Do not fire,” the orcs stopped when they saw the muzzles. From a distance, they crouched low. No one knew what the gesture meant. But no one called it a threat. Even after they withdrew, the cloth-covered bodies remained below in the gorge.

The meeting did not end. It could not. Dubois recorded a formal objection. Menon recorded one as well. Ben Youssef stipulated that the wounded receive mandatory priority. Han Doyun issued the final order.

Emergency distribution of locally fallen combatants’ remains, following restricted heat treatment, to the wounded and a portion of combat-capable personnel. Notification of infection and toxicity risks. Responsible officer: Han Doyun.

The statement explained everything and justified nothing.

Kenji had been listening outside the meeting. He had not entered. When it ended, Han Doyun called him over.

“Kenji.”

Kenji looked up.

“Don’t eat it.”

“Why just me?”

“You have maintenance work to do.”

“Will eating it keep me from doing maintenance?”

Han Doyun did not answer.

Kenji studied him for a long moment, then spoke.

“I won’t eat it. But not for that reason.”

Han Doyun nodded. A few clipped words of English passed between them. They sounded more like commands. Yujin did not write those words down. Sharing the same operational language did not mean sharing responsibility equally.

The preparation took place over a small brazier outside the tent. No one used the word cooking. Dubois objected to the very end, then finally designated a contamination zone. Her face remained rigid as she gave instructions, aware that those instructions were helping the work proceed. Ben Youssef confirmed that the wounded would receive the first portions. That confirmation remained as her consent.

Menon stayed outside the tent. He tried not to watch, but knew that not watching was also part of the record. Yujin could not bring himself to lift the camera. He listened instead. A knife slicing through wet tissue, a metal pot being set on stone, someone retching.

No one said they looked like pigs. Everyone had already thought it. Thoughts did their work even when left unspoken. On a battlefield, thoughts like those pushed people forward by degrees. They kill us. There are too many of them. We cannot reason with them. They look like pigs. With every added sentence, the forbidden line sank a little lower.

The first bowl went to the wounded. Ben Youssef held the patient’s hand and fed him. He could not chew properly. He swallowed only a little broth. The second bowl went to those still fit to fight. Those who ate did not look at one another. Neither did those who refused. The smell was more familiar than expected. That was the hardest thing to bear.

Han Doyun held the last remaining bowl. He did not raise it to his lips. After a long while, he set it on the ground.

“Captain, aren’t you going to eat?” someone asked.

Han Doyun shook his head.

“I gave the order.”

It was not an explanation. Nor was it punishment. It was the posture left behind when the word responsibility arrived too late.

The rain went on falling.

The brazier nearly went out several times, and each time someone bent over it and coaxed it back to life. No one celebrated the meal. No one made a joke. Only the words we have to survive drifted unspoken between the tents.

chapters.title: 22. Silence
chapters.markdown:
# 22. Silence

![Chapter 22 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-22.webp)


The next morning, someone laughed.

The laughter was brief. The radio had come back on. Kenji had forcibly wired a robot sensor module he had stripped down overnight into the relay’s auxiliary circuit, and the signal had climbed from one bar to two. A message appeared in one corner of the screen: ORBITAL RECEPTION CONFIRMED.

That one line made the air inside the tent feel a little lighter.

“See?” the signals operator spoke.

“We’re not dead yet.”

No one laughed aloud, but a few mouths twitched. The people who had eaten the night before were still alive. One casualty’s fever had come down slightly, and another had managed to swallow water. Those facts gave everyone false hope. No one knew yet that it was false.

Dubois did not trust that hope.

“Monitor everyone who ingested it. Temperature every four hours. Palpate the lymph nodes. Record coughing, chills, and skin lesions.”

“There are no symptoms yet,” a soldier spoke.

“That’s why we’re monitoring them.”

She marked those who had eaten separately from those who had not. Red and gray. Kenji was gray. He scowled at the color.

“Are the people who didn’t eat being quarantined too?”

“You used the same utensils, the same water, the same space.”

“I didn’t even go near that pot.”

“It was still the same space,” the answer was fair, but it offered no comfort. Quarantine had no interest in personal innocence. It considered only pathways and probabilities. That was why quarantine sometimes felt more inhuman than war. War chose its enemy; infection asked only whether you had been nearby.

Yujin stepped outside the tent. The rain had stopped. The Red Forest looked as though it had been washed clean, and the mist above the gorge had lifted a little. In the distance, an orc horn sounded once. No one could tell whether it signaled an attack or a funeral. Earth forces logged it as a threat.

Han Doyun was digging a drainage trench around the quarantine tent beside the armored vehicle. The rain had stopped, but the water that had seeped beneath the tent was not draining away. The engineers were out repairing the relay, and anyone with a free hand took up a shovel regardless of rank. The wet soil collapsed a little each time he cut into it. Without a word, he dug the same ground again.

“You didn’t eat?” Yujin asked.

“No.”

“Why not?”

Han Doyun looked down at the channel he had just dug.

“Because someone had to make the decisions.”

“You think that absolves you?”

He looked up. His eyes were tired.

“No.”

The answer came quickly.

“Then why did you order it documented?”

“So I wouldn’t be absolved.” Yujin asked nothing more. Not because the answer was enough. The longer he filmed Han Doyun’s exhaustion and fear, the more it seemed the people lying behind the quarantine sheeting because of his order would be pushed out of frame. Understanding the face of the person responsible was not the same as diminishing that responsibility. But in edited footage, the two often became the same thing. Yujin lowered the camera.

That afternoon, a small drop succeeded. It was not food. Batteries, antibiotics, painkillers, disinfectant, blood substitute, filters. The cargo drone dropped the crates onto a broad stretch of stone at the mouth of the gorge, and the soldiers ran out and dragged them back. One crate broke open, but most of its contents were recovered. For a moment, the soldiers grew talkative at the sight of the writing from Earth on the sides of the crates. Country of manufacture, expiration date, handling precautions, prevent foreign-matter contamination. Such phrases carried, strangely, the scent of home.

“Food will be in the next drop.”

The reply came from orbit.

Next.

The word was used too often here. The next drop, the next extraction, the next window, the next order. For people starving now, next was always too far away.

Near sunset, the first case of high fever appeared.

He was a soldier who had eaten a second bowl the night before. At first, he complained of being cold. They raised the temperature of his powered suit’s lining, but the shaking would not stop. His temperature climbed above thirty-nine degrees. When Ben Youssef touched his neck, the soldier fought back a scream.

“Lymph nodes,” Dubois spoke.

Her voice dropped.

The areas beneath his neck and under his arms were swollen a dark reddish black. They looked hard and painful. The soldier kept saying he was cold. His fingertips were hot, and his lips were dry. There were no lesions on his face yet. That made it more ominous. Whatever it was had begun inside before becoming visible.

“How many hours since ingestion?”

“Thirty-one.”

“Too fast.”

“But it’s started,” Ben Youssef spoke.

Dubois opened a specimen kit. Blood, lymphatic fluid, an oral swab, a skin-surface sample. The patient cursed as the needle went in, then immediately apologized. There was no need to apologize. He did anyway. Soldiers often used their most polite voices when they were in pain.

The laughter vanished from the tent. No one mentioned the brief relief they had felt when the radio came back on a few hours earlier. Those who had eaten felt their necks and underarms. Those who had not did the same.

Kenji looked down at his hands. Red soil was packed beneath his fingernails. With those hands, he had touched the relay, the water containers, and the stretchers carrying the wounded.

“Can I catch it even if I didn’t eat?” he asked.

Dubois could not answer at once.

Her silence was worse than an answer.

By nightfall, the tent had been divided twice more. Those who had ingested it and those who had not, symptomatic and asymptomatic. But there was not enough space. The plastic sheeting was too short, the tape was wet, and the patients coughed. Dubois ordered the medical robot to repeat the disinfection procedure. The robot followed its instructions, but it meant nothing whenever someone passed through and lifted the sheeting.

A request for analysis came down from the orbiter. Could they send the samples up? Dubois sent her reply.

Impossible. Field quarantine takes priority until the front is sealed.

A few minutes later, another question arrived.

Request status confirmation of emergency evacuees.

For the first time, Dubois’s face went completely rigid when she saw the message. She called Han Doyun over.

“There were wounded we sent up before restricted cooking began.”

“They didn’t eat.”

“Two were drenched in local blood during close combat, and one handled the bodies.”

Han Doyun looked through the quarantine sheeting.

“If it spreads not only through ingestion but through bodily fluids as well. . . .”

“They’re already aboard the orbiter.”

This time, too, the silence was worse than an answer.

chapters.title: 23. The Fifteenth Day
chapters.markdown:
# 23. The Fifteenth Day

![Chapter 23 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-23.webp)

The lymph nodes swelled like dark crimson stones.

The first patient would not let anyone touch his neck. He twisted away whenever a hand came near. The second clutched his armpit and curled in on himself. In the third, the cough came before the fever. It was dry at first, then flecked with blood a few hours later. The blood was not bright red, but dark and viscous. Once it stained the inside of a mask, it did not come off easily.

Dubois lost all expression. She did not get angry or blame anyone. There was no time. Samples, temperatures, contacts, amounts consumed, cooking utensils, water containers, order of distribution, routes taken by the wounded. Everything became a record. Records were not treatment, but treatment could not begin without them. She knew that cruel sequence.

“Possible pulmonary phase,” she said it quietly.

Ben Youssef fitted an oxygen mask over the patient’s face.

“Transmission?”

“We don’t know.”

“Best estimate.”

“Short-range droplets are possible.”

Those words divided the tent in two. The distinction between those who had eaten and those who had not was no longer enough. Had they stood beside someone who coughed? Touched the same mask? Held the same water container? Carried a stretcher in the same gloves? Held a rifle in those same gloves? Who had touched the cloth used to clean the rifle?

Yujin wiped his camera lens. It was fogged on the inside. He could not tell whether it was from his own breath or the disinfectant in the tent. He filmed from behind the isolation screen. He did not film the patients’ faces. He filmed their hands and masks, their swollen necks, the bed numbers marked in red. If he filmed their faces, viewers on Earth would pity them. If he filmed their hands, they would have to think about what had happened.

Han Doyun stopped in front of the isolation screen.

“How many are combat-capable?”

“Are you asking medically or militarily?” Ben Youssef said.

“Both.”

“Both answers are bad.”

She handed him the list. Eleven symptomatic out of nineteen who had eaten. Two fevers among those who had not. Three symptomatic among the wounded. Isolation recommended for all contacts.

All.

The word meant the entire forward company.

“Then is this the end of us here?” Han Doyun asked.

Ben Youssef did not answer. Instead, she opened the patient’s oxygen valve a little farther. There was not much oxygen left either.

At first, the orbiter requested data. Temperature curves, blood images, lymphatic-fluid samples, footage of respiratory symptoms. Dubois sent them. The transmission rate was low, and the files cut out repeatedly. A single fragment of video took several minutes to send. Even during those minutes, the patient’s temperature continued to rise.

A few minutes later, another channel opened from the orbital medical bay.

“Forward unit, confirm. Eleven evacuees who were asymptomatic before transport are currently in the orbital medical bay.”

Everyone in the tent went still.

Those eleven were wounded personnel sent up the previous night and the dawn before that. It had been before the meat was eaten. They had shown no symptoms. Emergency evacuation had been cleared under quarantine protocol, and four recovery-craft crew members had transported them. At the time, the decision had been obvious. Sending wounded personnel with unstable vital signs to the orbital medical bay was rescue. Now rescue and transmission belonged in the same sentence.

Dubois closed her eyes, then opened them.

“Seal the medical bay immediately.”

Vosrov’s voice came from orbit.

“Already under way.”

“Ventilation?”

“Being isolated.”

“Too late.”

Dubois was not accusing anyone. She was delivering a finding.

A schematic of the orbiter’s medical bay appeared on the screen. Three compartments were shaded red. Eleven evacuees, three medical officers, four recovery-craft crew members, two technicians who had manually dragged out a decontamination robot. The automatic doors were sealed, and the ventilation system was vented into space. It meant the doors could not be opened again. The orbiter had been built with the cleanest technology Earth possessed, but in being an enclosed space, it was no different from a medieval fortress.

Yujin filmed the screen. People became dots, rooms became colors. It resembled the refugee maps he had seen on the ground.

Vosrov spoke briefly over the command net.

“Suspend Earth-return procedures. All recovery craft remain on standby. Maintain the medical-bay lockdown. Reclassify all contacts aboard the orbiter.”

“What about Earth?” someone asked.

“Send only the data.”

The words reassured everyone and, at the same time, made them feel abandoned. Earth would not be infected. Earth would not save them either. Earth would receive the data.

The forward company came under attack that night. The orcs dropped rocks, burning cloth, and short spears from above the gorge. The Earth forces returned fire. But the hands holding the rifles trembled, and several soldiers coughed as they fired. The M240L remained terrifyingly powerful. Its rounds tore through rock and flesh. But the strength of a weapon did not make the person wielding it strong.

One soldier vomited while firing. Blood splattered the inside of his mask. The person beside him tried to pull him down and fell with him. The joints of their powered suits sounded warnings, long electronic wails amid gunfire, horns, and the coughing of the sick. The tactical net reclassified the soldier as combat-ineffective. One blue dot on the screen turned yellow.

Kenji developed a fever too. He had not eaten. Everyone knew it. That made it more frightening.

“I didn’t eat any,” he said.

“I know.”

Ben Youssef adjusted his mask.

“Then why?”

No one could answer. Shared cooking utensils, water, hands, coughing, soil, gloves. There were many possibilities and no certainty. Kenji refused to put down his maintenance tools. His fingers trembled, and he dropped a small wrench. He tried to pick it up, then gave up.

“The relay…” he said.

“Forget the relay,” Han Doyun said.

“It’s not finished yet.”

“Forget it.”

For the first time, Han Doyun did not sound as though he were giving an order.

On the fifteenth day, the forward company’s blue dots went dark one by one. Some meant death, some loss of communications, some loss of vital signs. From the orbiter’s screens, they could see the order in which they vanished. One dot turned gray, a few seconds later another turned yellow, and the thin lines around them broke. The entire battlefield looked like a recreation of some ancient plague map.

Dubois received the results of a comparison with Earth’s historical infectious-disease records. The words bubonic plague appeared on the screen. It was not, strictly speaking, that disease. The pathogen was different, the planet was different, the ecology was different. But the symptoms, the speed, and the transmission pattern in the pulmonary phase were too similar. It looked as though a medieval nightmare had passed through the red bodies of Mars and entered a space force tent.

“It isn’t the bubonic plague,” Dubois said.

“But it resembles it,” Ben Youssef replied.

“The resemblance alone is frightening enough.”

Han Doyun prepared his final report. He removed his own order, then put it back in.

Restricted cooking order. Responsible officer: Han Doyun.

Yujin watched the transmission-pending indicator and asked.

“If we make it back alive, there will be an investigation.”

“I know.”

“What will you say?”

Han Doyun looked in turn at the patients behind the isolation screen and the wounded lying outside it.

“I’ll say that, given the same information and circumstances, I would issue the same order.”

“But Dr. Dubois’s warning was right. Nineteen people ate because of your order, Captain, and the number of cases rose afterward.”

“I know.”

“You would still make the same choice?”

“At the time, I had men dying in front of me. There was no other food and no rescue time. If I went back, I would still try to save those people first.”

“What about the people who ate the meat and died?”

“They are my responsibility.”

“Don’t you regret it?”

“No.”

He did not delete the sentence bearing his name.

Menon’s determination that the orcs were sapient, Dubois’s quarantine warning, Ben Youssef’s authorization of the distribution, the coordinates of the supply failure, the orcs’ method of attacking the relay. Everything went into the same report.

The report was long, and time was short.

A horn sounded outside. This time it was close. Yujin checked the camera battery. Four percent. He began recording. On the screen, Han Doyun transmitted the report, raised his rifle, then lowered it again. These were not the movements of a man who did not know what to do first, but of one who knew that nothing he did would be enough.

Yujin filmed him. Then he spoke very softly.

“It’s been transmitted.”

Han Doyun nodded.

“Then it remains.”

Yujin did not ask whether he meant the people or the record.

chapters.title: 24. The Strategist on the Hill
chapters.markdown:
# 24. The Strategist on the Hill

![Chapter 24 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-24.webp)


On Nowak’s screen, failure was organized by color.

Red meant death and infection. Orange meant supply failure. Yellow meant unstable communications, blue meant equipment damage, and green marked areas for improvement. From a distance, the screen looked less like a war than a complex circuit diagram. The places where people had died, where drones had fallen, where orcs had smashed relays—they were all colors.

Seo Yujin stood looking at the screen for a long time.

“Are you drafting improvements for the next operation?”

Nowak did not look up.

“It’s an analysis chart of the frontline supply failures.”

“People are still inside the quarantine barrier.”

“We have to document where the chain broke while we can still ask the survivors. The equipment logs are disappearing too.”

Nowak opened one of the orange lines on the screen. It showed, in order, the time the last cargo drone strayed from its route, the coordinates where the relay went down, and the weight of the food they had failed to recover.

He spread his fingers over the map of the gorge. The landing zone, the Citadel Belt, the Southern Gorge, the Green Corridor, the drone drop points, the relay loss points. The cleaner the map, the more distant the actual field became. A small gray circle marked the frontline company’s last position. It bore overlapping designations: combat ineffective, infected, communications lost, presumed dead.

“Relay redundancy. Countermeasures against landing-marker concealment. Diversified cargo-drone routes. Separate loading of helicopter fuel. Increased frontline food allowance. Expansion of quarantine barriers.”

He read them one by one.

“Next time, we can save them.”

“Next time,” Yujin said.

Only then did Nowak look up. His eyes were bloodshot. They were the eyes of a man who had not slept properly in days. He was not a cold man. He was a man assigned to do cold work.

“For the sake of those who have just died, we have to save them next time.”

He meant it. Yujin knew that. That made it worse. Sincerity could become fuel for the next invasion. A vow not to let someone’s death be in vain could sometimes become an order to pave the same road wider.

Hale received the same report at the temporary command post. He listened to the frontline company’s final transmission three times. Captain Han Doyun’s voice was ragged, punctuated by coughing and gunfire. Restricted cooking order, supply-route coordinates, orc tactics, time of outbreak, quarantine recommendation. The report ended not as a commander’s attempt to justify himself, but as material for the next operation.

“He left behind responsibility,” Yujin said.

Hale did not take his eyes off the screen.

“Responsibility does not stop an operation.”

“Maybe it should.”

“That decision is beyond my authority.”

It sounded like evasion, but within the system, it was true. Hale was a battalion commander. A battalion commander did not decide the reason for a war. He simply moved people when that reason came down as an order. Everyone in this system pointed beyond the limits of their own authority. Commanders pointed to politicians, politicians to public opinion and the right to survival, corporations to contracts and shareholders, scientists to the bounds of medical expertise, journalists to security classifications. Everything beyond one person’s authority gathered to form the center of authority itself.

Aboard the orbiter, Colonel Elena Vosrov received a report on the medical section lockdown. The biosigns inside the red section were dwindling. They could not open the door. If they did, the entire orbiter would be at risk. If they kept it shut, the people inside would die.

“Automated disinfection?”

“In progress.”

“Patient status?”

The medical officer looked at the screen before answering.

“Two dead. Four critical. The rest have fevers.”

Vosrov did not record the numbers. They were already on the screen. Instead, she recorded the decision.

Maintain medical section lockdown. No return to Earth. Seal samples in orbit. Transmit data only.

Her hand did not tremble. A steady hand did not mean a steady heart. A spacecraft commander’s hand was not allowed to tremble. Docking, quarantine, orbital correction, oxygen circulation—none of them tolerated a shaking hand.

At the end of the meeting, Dr. Ravi Menon’s report was submitted. Possible indigenous intelligent species, burial markers, refugee vessel, farmland and waterways, the white flag incident. Dr. Claire Dubois’s report was submitted as well. Warning against consuming indigenous organisms, suspected contamination routes, possible droplet transmission during the pulmonary phase, quarantine recommendation.

Nowak’s improvement plan was the body of the report. Menon’s and Dubois’s reports were attachments.

Yujin looked at the order.

“Can you change the order?”

Vosrov looked at him wearily.

“It’s an operational report.”

“Exactly.”

“The body of an operational report contains what is needed for the next operation.”

She was correct. And within that correctness, everything was decided. The assessment of an intelligent species was an appendix. The ecological damage was an appendix. The analysis that the Black Ship had saved a refugee vessel was an appendix. The body was drones and fuel and vaccines and corridors.

Outside, the Martian night revolved below. Each time the orbiter circled the planet, it passed over the landing zone and the Citadel Belt, the Inland Sea where the Black Ship had sunk, and the gorge where the frontline company had vanished. The image remained perfectly clear.

So clear that no one could say they had not known.

chapters.title: 25. The Dead Landing Zone
chapters.markdown:
# 25. The Dead Landing Zone

![Chapter 25 Illustration](resources/assets/chapter-25.webp)

Empty helmets lay inside the landing zone’s white quarantine line.

At first, they looked as though someone had simply taken them off and left them there. But the helmets stood in rows, each bearing a numbered tag. Disinfected. Awaiting disposal. Do not retrieve. A thin layer of red dust settled over the visors. Whenever the wind blew, the tags stirred slightly. The name labels inside had been removed. With names attached, they looked less like waste and more like personal effects.

Seo Yujin filmed the scene from outside the quarantine line. The landing zone was far quieter than when he had first arrived. Some of the armored vehicles were in the Citadel Belt; others sat idle beneath the maintenance shelters. An Apache lay with its rotors removed. A Black Hawk had been sealed off after a medical evacuation. Two decontamination robots moved slowly across the ground. The air smelled of bleach, Martian soil, and fuel.

With the people gone, the machinery sounded louder. Ventilation units, chargers, remote cranes, quarantine blowers, the feet of robots moving slowly. A military base ordinarily lived by its noise. But without human voices, that noise became the sound of ruins.

An emergency personnel-accountability announcement repeated over Yujin’s headset. It was an automated broadcast searching for people still unaccounted for after the outbreak.

 － Unaccounted personnel, respond. Report your current location. －

There was no answer. A moment later, the same sentence played again. The voice neither hurried nor tired.

 － Unaccounted personnel, respond. Report your current location. －

Yujin removed the receiver covering one ear. The voice did not disappear. The broadcast towers outside the landing zone were carrying the same message. The voice that had sounded small inside his headset spread far across the red plain and between the empty maintenance shelters.

 － Unaccounted personnel, respond. Report your current location. －

As power to the quarantine sectors was disconnected one by one, the broadcast towers went silent in turn. The most distant voice vanished first. The tower above the maintenance shelter called for the same people several more times. Yujin turned his camera toward it, but all the frame captured was the white quarantine barrier and a closed door.

Unaccounted personnel, respond. Report your current—

The final broadcast cut off in the middle of the sentence. The ventilation units and blowers kept running, but only then did the landing zone become completely silent.

Sato Akira was gone. He had not been sent to the front, but he had been quarantined because his filming equipment had come into contact with evacuees from orbit. He had no symptoms. He was quarantined anyway. Yujin received a message from him.

 － Alive. Four camera batteries left. Camera may outlast me. －

Yujin could not write a reply. Anything he said seemed likely to kill the joke. He picked up the terminal, then set it down. A few minutes later, he sent a short message.

 － Stay alive. －

Akira’s reply came late.

 － If that’s an order. －

Yujin could not laugh when he read it.

In the temporary archive, he reviewed his original footage again. The white flag. The small body collapsing as it tried to pick up the flag. Cavalry falling beneath the flares. A hand rubbing a black root beside the Green Corridor. The Black Ship on the Inland Sea. Masked soldiers inside the forward quarantine barrier. Captain Han Doyun’s final report. Sergeant Nakamura Kenji’s trembling hand.

It was all there.

Almost none of it could be released.

A message arrived from Li Wei.

－ All original footage subject to security review. Preservation in the official record guaranteed. Release date undetermined. －

The words resembled a grave. Preserved, but unseen.

Yujin opened the footage of the Black Ship. The ship was still turning toward the side it could not defeat. It was the same no matter how many times he watched. The landing craft were strong, and the Black Ship was weak. Yet the outcome was not so simple. The refugee boats had escaped. The report called it a failure to pursue. In Yujin’s original footage, it looked like a successful rescue. Of course, those words could never appear in an Earth forces report.

He watched the white-flag footage again. The warning had been broadcast in four languages, and the orcs had not stopped. The small body had tried to pick up the flag. A shot rang out. The phrase accidental discharge became too small when laid over that scene. Accident could explain the instant the trigger was pulled. It could not explain the long chain of time that had brought that muzzle there.

Dr. Ravi Menon approached from beyond the quarantine line.

“Do you still have it?”

“Yes.”

“Copies?”

Yujin did not answer.

Menon understood.

“I kept a separate copy of my original report too.”

“Can you release it?”

“Probably not.”

“Then why keep it?”

Menon looked at the empty helmets.

“So that later, when someone lies, I can at least make sure my memory wasn’t wrong.”

The words were small, almost powerless. But Yujin understood them. Records could not save the world. Without them, though, the world could deceive itself more easily.

At the far end of the landing zone, combat engineers were inspecting the Green Corridor equipment. Even amid quarantine and withdrawal, the equipment had not stopped. The reason was simple. It was settlement infrastructure, and settlement infrastructure was exempt from operational suspension. The cultivation mats drank in water and darkened. Little by little, more green film spread across the red soil. The people were quarantined, and the moss grew.

Menon looked toward it.

“That’s alive too.”

“Yes.”

“That’s what makes it harder. This isn’t an invasion by dead machines. It’s a living invasion.”

Yujin filmed that scene as well. The quarantine line, the empty helmets, the Green Corridor. When he tried to fit them into a single frame, the composition would not work. He stepped back. From farther away, everything fit. But the farther he went, the smaller the people became.

There was now one more piece of footage no one would ever see.

chapters.title: 26. Wreckage
chapters.markdown:
# 26. Wreckage

![Chapter 26 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-26.webp)

A sealed specimen case sat beside a decommissioned quadruped robot.

Both were the same gray. One had lost its legs on the battlefield; the other held what had been brought back from it. Empty sockets gaped along the robot’s flank where Kenji had stripped out parts. The specimen case bore three layers of seals and a red warning label.

Biological hazard. Removal from orbit prohibited.

Dubois checked the signatures in front of the case. Her hands had grown raw even inside her gloves. She had changed them too often over the past several days. A small cut marked the back of one hand, covered by a transparent waterproof film.

“Aren’t you sending it to Earth?” Yujin asked.

“Only the data.”

“Wouldn’t it be faster with the specimen?”

“Keeping it from spreading comes before speed.”

Dubois did not place her hand on the case. Not touching was part of her profession.

“We are already late enough. We can afford to be later.” It was the first time she had spoken in a way that blamed herself. She had tried to stop it, kept records, filed her objections. But the disease had begun. The fact that her warnings had been right offered no comfort. It meant the very thing she had warned of had come to pass.

The wreckage inventory was long. Seventeen drones lost. Five quadruped supply robots decommissioned or unrecoverable. One bipedal work robot critically damaged. One Black Hawk sealed off. One Apache down for extended maintenance. Six relays lost. Four solar membranes destroyed by fire. Eleven irrigation pipes ruptured. Two armored vehicles under movement restrictions. Numerous forward detachment personnel missing, dead, or in isolation.

Nowak did not shorten the list. If he did, the next person would make the same mistake.

“Wreckage is logistics too,” he said.

“What do you mean?”

“We need to know what broke so we know what to bring next time.”

Next time.

The words now sounded like a funeral bell.

From the orbiter, Vosrov watched the ground wreckage and the quarantine status of the medical section at the same time. The number of biosignals inside the medical section was dwindling. Outside, technicians rerouted the wiring connected to the sealed section. A spacecraft was built for people, but sometimes it had to shut people away to keep moving. The automatic doors had been designed to protect people. Now they confined them.

“Medical section three fully isolated.”

“Confirmed.”

“Two survivors inside.”

“Status.”

“Critical. Direct access impossible.”

Vosrov did not close her eyes. Looking away from the screen would have been the same as refusing to decide.

“Continue remote medication.”

“Limited effect.”

“Continue.”

What went to Earth was not people, but data. Blood images, estimated protein structures, genetic fragments, an outbreak timeline, contact routes, casualty lists, equipment loss tables. Data traveled at the speed of light. People could not. The order prohibiting return to Earth remained in force.

Yujin looked at the casualty list. There were names. There were nationalities too. American, German, French, Polish, Korean, Canadian, Indian, British, Australian. Their multinational character was visible even on the list. But the authorizing signatures at the top narrowed to a handful of countries and corporations. Death had been distributed broadly; decision-making power had been concentrated narrowly.

Captain Han Doyun was officially presumed dead after being listed as missing. His last biosignal had cut out eleven minutes after he transmitted the forward company report. His final file contained his own order. Restricted preparation order. Officer responsible: Han Doyun.

Nineteen people had eaten the meat under that order. Seven died from red swellings and the complications that followed, while twelve survived. Five of the survivors had been suffering from severe hypoglycemia, dehydration, and post-injury debilitation when they were rescued. In cautious language, the medical records stated that without that meal, they might not have lasted until recovery. For some, the same order marked the beginning of infection. For others, it bought the day they needed to reach the rescue craft.

Kenji was alive. He had not eaten the meat, but he had been infected, and had barely stabilized after receiving a candidate antiserum. His hands still trembled. In the recovery ward, he said to Yujin,

“The story must not become a better one just because one sergeant survived.”

Yujin did not record him.

“I won’t write it that way.”

“Can you?”

Yujin could not answer.

After a long while, Kenji spoke again.

“Was the captain a bad man?”

Yujin could not answer at once. The question was waiting for an answer that was too easy.

“He gave a bad order.”

“I know that.”

“I don’t think I should write more than that.”

Kenji nodded. He knew it too. Understanding a person must not become a way of erasing responsibility. But without understanding, there was no way to know how the same responsibility came to be repeated.

The wreckage remained on the ground, in orbit, and in the reports. But what the wreckage meant soon began to change. The decommissioned robot became the rationale for improvements to the next model. The sealed specimen became the starting point for vaccine development. The casualty list became the basis for hazard pay, posthumous decorations, and classification levels.

Defeat lost its name and became redesign.

chapters.title: 27. A Report, Not an Epilogue
chapters.markdown:
# 27. A Report, Not an Epilogue

![Chapter 27 Illustration](resources/assets/chapter-27.webp)

The report had a main body and appendices.

The main body was forty-two pages long. Causes of supply failure, loss of relay units, operational limits of drones, the need to transport helicopter fuel in separate loads, increased frontline food allowances, expanded quarantine equipment, a request for vaccine development, plans to widen the Green Corridor. The sentences were short and clear. Anyone who read them would know what more to bring next time.

The appendices ran to more than three hundred pages. The white flag incident, the possibility of an indigenous intelligent species, funerary markers, farmland and waterways, refugee boats, an analysis of the Black Ship’s actions, warnings against consuming indigenous organisms, the early progression of the red swelling, a catalog of Yujin’s footage. The appendices were longer than the main body, but the decisions lay in the main body.

Yujin looked at the file structure and said,

“The order is the conclusion.”

Vosrov looked tired.

“Reports are structured to be read.”

“Deciding what gets read is part of the structure.”

She did not answer.

The remaining command staff, the scientific survey team, and the Earth Liaison Committee were in the conference room. The representatives from Earth sat in immaculate rooms on the screens. Neither the queues at Sriharikota nor the quarantine lines on Mars were visible. Flags and corporate logos stood in the background. The list of participants contained more agency names than country names: the Migration Security Agency, the Orbital Transport Union, the Settlement Insurance Authority, the International Joint Press Corps, the Civilian-Military Logistics Consortium. Earth always divided its names until responsibility wore thin.

Dubois spoke.

“The prohibition on consuming indigenous organisms must be elevated to an absolute provision. It must account for contact with indigenous bodily fluids, cooking utensils, shared water, and the possibility of droplet transmission during the pulmonary stage.”

One representative asked,

“Is vaccine development feasible?”

“Yes. We need time.”

“Then does that mean operations can resume after tighter quarantine measures and vaccination?”

Dubois paused.

“Medically, it means we can reduce the risk.”

“We’ll record that as indicating the possibility of resuming operations.”

She closed her mouth. A medical sentence had been translated into a military one. The translation was not wrong, which made it difficult to challenge.

Then it was Menon’s turn. He read the assessment of the indigenous intelligent species. Citadels, military standards, funerals, agriculture, evacuation, the sacrificial action of the coastal warship. His voice did not waver. But the representatives on the screens looked at other materials from time to time. Some were looking at the vaccine schedule. Others were looking at the cost of expanding the Green Corridor.

“Is negotiation possible?” someone asked.

“We need to analyze their language system. But first, hostilities must cease.”

“That is impossible at this time,” Hale said.

Menon looked at him. Hale did not look away.

“They attack us too.”

“We went in first.”

“That judgment is outside my authority.”

The same sentence again. Outside my authority. Many things were decided beyond it, and many people died within it.

Nowak’s proposed improvements passed quickly. More relay units, spoof-resistant landing markers, increased drone cargo capacity, distributed helicopter fuel supplies, increased frontline food allowances, additional quarantine barrier modules, a reserve Black Hawk dedicated to recovery missions, and expanded equipment for maintaining the Green Corridor.

“Expanding the Green Corridor will increase ecological damage,” Menon said.

The chief engineer replied,

“Without the corridor, we cannot maintain the supply route.”

“That supply route sustains the invasion.”

The conference room fell silent. The sentence was too direct. Direct sentences did not survive long in meetings. Soon someone proposed revising the language. The word invasion was replaced with follow-up settlement security mission.

The final conclusion was read in a cold voice.

The First Mars Landing Operation was suspended due to unforeseen indigenous biological hazards and vulnerabilities in the forward supply network. It nevertheless yielded strategic gains: securing the landing zone, penetrating the Citadel Belt, achieving initial stabilization of the ecological starter biome, classifying indigenous hazards, and obtaining response data on the red swelling. Follow-up operations will be prepared for the next low-energy launch window with reinforced quarantine, logistics, and medical systems.

Suspended.

Yujin heard the word. Suspended did not mean over. It meant resting, not stopping.

After the meeting, Vosrov signed the order barring return to Earth once again. The samples would remain in orbit, the people would remain in quarantine, and only the report would go to Earth. On Earth, that report would be summarized. The summary would become a press release, the press release would become news captions, and the news captions would pass between stock prices, migration eligibility reviews, and campaign slogans.

The First Expedition had fallen to disease. The landing zone stood empty, and return to Earth had been forbidden. It looked like the sort of scene that might mark the end of a war. But in Earth’s documents, disease was not an ending. It was classified as a defect to be corrected. It became proof that they could go back once they had developed a vaccine, tightened quarantine, and increased supplies.

Yujin looked at the report’s title.

Post-Action Analysis of the First Mars Landing Operation and Recommendations for Follow-Up Settlement Security.

It was not an epilogue.

chapters.title: 28. The Sealed Original Footage
chapters.markdown:
# 28. The Sealed Original Footage

![Chapter 28 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-28.webp)

A red seal appeared on Yujin’s storage device.

It was not a physical seal. It was an icon on the screen of a small terminal. But in one sense, it was stronger: there was nothing he could tear off with his hands. All the original footage had been placed under a security classification. Access was limited to operational command, the United Nations Migration Security Agency, the designated scientific review panel, and the legal review panel. As an embedded journalist, Yujin had lost formal access to his own footage.

He stared at the notice for a long time. The screen was helpful. It gave the reason for the change in access, the retention period, the appeals procedure, the department responsible, the estimated response time for an automated reply. Everything was there. Everything except the footage.

Akira sent a message from the quarantine section.

It’s our footage, but it isn’t ours.

Yujin replied:

Maybe it never was.

He regretted it as soon as he sent it. It sounded too much like a sentence. The real feeling was shorter and messier. Closer to a curse, a sigh, or the silence of sending nothing at all. He turned the terminal off and on again. The seal remained.

Li Wei opened a channel from Earth.

“Mr. Seo, a separate edited version will be provided for the official documentary.”

“What about my original footage?”

“It will be preserved.”

“Will it be released?”

“No date has been set.”

“Then it isn’t being preserved. It’s being buried.”

Li Wei did not answer at once. On the screen, he looked older than before. The lighting in the Sriharikota public affairs office was as clean as ever, but there were dark shadows under his eyes. Beyond the glass wall behind him, Yujin could see a conference room. People moved back and forth, and a cargo-ship schedule was displayed on a screen. Earth was already preparing what it would say next.

“I’ve seen the original footage too,” Li Wei said.

“So you know.”

“I do.”

“And you’re still blocking it?”

“I’m not the one blocking it.”

“Everyone says that.”

Li Wei lowered his head. He did not get angry. Yujin would have found it easier if he had. Angry people were easy to deal with. People who understood their roles precisely were harder.

“The Korean side doesn’t want it released either.”

Yujin looked at the screen.

“Why?”

“Because of public opinion at home. There’s the part where a former 707 officer ordered rationing, and the fact that equipment from Korean companies was used in the corridor facilities and communications network. The government wants to say that Korea provided humanitarian aid and made a technological contribution.”

“Isn’t that a distortion?”

“Some of it is true.”

“That makes it worse.”

Li Wei had no answer.

Korea was not a benevolent observer in this story. Neither was Yujin. He had made the record, but that record existed within the language, platforms, and security classifications of the developed world. Han Doyun knew war and gave the orders anyway. Kenji had not eaten, but he had maintained equipment within the same system and contracted the same disease. The UN strategic communications office had not invented new lies. It had merely translated the words everyone already used into administrative prose anyone could understand.

Yujin listened again to the narration he had recorded in his own voice. Humanity’s new living space. Settlement support. Securing safety. Local hazards. He had read those words aloud. At first he had believed them; later he had doubted them; and still he had kept reading. A journalist stood behind the camera, but he did not decide alone where it pointed.

The list of sealed originals contained 642 files. The White Flag Incident. The Flare Battle. Green Corridor. Coastal Evacuation. Black Ship. Forward Quarantine. Final Report. Landing Zone Wreckage.

Yujin selected one file. It was Han Doyun’s final report. Access denied. He had already watched it once, saved it once, and lost it once.

A security notice appeared on the screen.

This material contains sensitive information related to the stability of future operations.

“Stability.”

Yujin laughed without making a sound. The word held many things. The stability that kept soldiers from starving again. The stability that kept vaccine cold chains from breaking. The stability that kept public opinion from demanding an end to the operation. The stability that kept investors from pulling out. The stability in which the red marshes of Mars vanished beneath the Green Corridor.

He created a new file. It was an article that could not be published. He took a long time to choose the title. In the end, he kept it short.

The Invasion of Mars.

Then he wrote the first sentence.

It was not that we did not know they were people.

That sentence would not be published either. Still, he wrote it. Sometimes only the person doing the writing knew the difference between preservation and burial.

He continued. The white flag had not been a misunderstanding. The Black Ship had not been a reckless attack. The red swellings had not been punishment from heaven. They were the product of failed supply lines, orders, hunger, and the old habit of refusing to see the other side as human. And those who already knew all of this had classified every fact as a manageable risk.

The longer the sentences grew, the less Yujin knew whether he was writing fiction or journalism. Perhaps it was neither. Perhaps it was only an annotation left beside a list of sealed files, an annotation no one had permission to read.

chapters.title: 29. The Vaccine and the Corridor
chapters.markdown:
# 29. The Vaccine and the Corridor

![Chapter 29 illustration](resources/assets/chapter-29.webp)

The liquid inside the incubator was nearly transparent.

In the adjoining hangar, the starter cultures were a vivid green. Both consignments appeared on the same temperature-control manifest for the same day. One was a candidate antiserum intended to prevent the Red Swelling. The other was moss intended to turn the red soil of Mars into Earth-like soil.

Dr. Claire Dubois studied the arrangement in silence for a long time.

“I told you not to keep them together.”
